name: ATSAMD21G18A-MU
title: SAM D21/DA1 family: low-power Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 48 MHz, up to 256 KB Flash and 32 KB SRAM, full-speed USB, 12-bit ADC, 10-bit DAC, capacitive touch
summary: A family of 32-bit microcontrollers built on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core at up to 48 MHz, in 32- to 64-pin packages with 16 KB to 256 KB of Flash and 4 KB to 32 KB of SRAM. Around the core sit a 12-channel DMA controller and event system, up to six SERCOM serial blocks, up to five 16-bit TCs and four TCCs, a full-speed USB 2.0 host and device, a two-channel I2S, a 12-bit 350 ksps ADC, a 10-bit DAC, up to four comparators and a touch controller. The ATSAMD21G18A-MU is the 48-pin VQFN member with 256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM and 38 I/O pins, graded for -40 °C to 85 °C, running from a single 1.62 V to 3.63 V supply.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ (r0p1), up to 48 MHz, single-cycle multiplier, Micro Trace Buffer
256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM; no RWWEE section on 256 KB devices
16 KB to 256 KB Flash, 4 KB to 32 KB SRAM
SAM D21 1.62 V to 3.63 V; SAM DA1 2.7 V to 3.63 V; internal regulator gives VDDCORE 1.2 V
12-bit, 350 ksps, up to 20 channels (14 on the 48-pin A part), gain 1/2x to 16x, 16-bit by oversampling
full-speed 12 Mbps USB 2.0, embedded host and device, eight endpoints
up to six SERCOM (USART, I2C up to 3.4 MHz, SPI, LIN client), one two-channel I2S
up to five 16-bit TC, up to four 24-bit/16-bit TCC, 32-bit RTC, WDT
PTC, up to 256 mutual-capacitance channels (120/10 on the 48-pin A part)

tables.title: PORT function multiplexing for SAM D21 A/B/C/D variant devices and SAM DA1 A/B variant devices
notes: (1) The WLCSP45 package follows the SAMD21J multiplexing.
(2) Every analog function sits on peripheral function B; selecting B also turns off the digital control of the pin.
(3) SERCOM I2C mode works on a subset of pins only (see SERCOM pins supporting I2C).
(4) TC6 and TC7 do not exist on SAM D21E and SAM D21G.
(5) SWDIO becomes active only while a debugger is present.
(6) PA24 and PA25 have no drive-strength option. Left unconnected, they should be set as inputs with the pull-up on, so a floating pad does not draw extra current (under 1 mA).
(7) SERCOM4 and SERCOM5 are absent on SAMD21ExxA, on SAMD21E15 and SAMD21E16 in variants B, BU, CU and L, and on SAMD21E17 in variants D, DU and L.
(8) TCC3 exists only on SAMD21x17D.

tables.title: PORT function multiplexing for L variant devices
notes: (1) Every analog function sits on peripheral function B; selecting B also turns off the digital control of the pin.
(2) SERCOM I2C mode works on a subset of pins only.
(3) TC6 and TC7 do not exist on SAM D21E.
(4) SWDIO becomes active only while a debugger is present.
(5) PA24 and PA25 have no drive-strength option; left unconnected, they should be inputs with the pull-up on to avoid extra current (under 1 mA) from a floating pad.
(6) TC6 exists on SAM D21GxL only, not on SAM D21ExL.
(7) SERCOM4 and SERCOM5 are absent on SAM D21E devices.
(8) TCC3 exists only on SAMD21x17L devices.
SWDIO(5) should read SWDIO(4).

circuits.title: Power supply connection
circuits.description: One main rail of 1.62 V to 3.63 V feeds VDDIO, VDDANA and VDDIN together, with a capacitor from that rail to ground. VDDCORE, the 1.2 V regulator output, has its own capacitor to ground. GND and GNDANA both go to the board ground.

circuits.title: Current consumption measurement setup
circuits.description: The supply current is measured by one meter feeding VDDIN, VDDANA and VDDIO together; VDDCORE, the regulator output, has only its decoupling capacitor to ground.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connection
circuits.description: A crystal sits between XIN (PA14) and XOUT (PA15), each pin with its own load capacitor CLEXT to ground. CSTRAY is the board capacitance between the two lines. CLEXT is sized with the load capacitance equation so the crystal sees its specified CL. The 32 kHz oscillator on XIN32 and XOUT32 is connected the same way.

parts.note: modelled as LM, CM and RM in series with CSHUNT across them

circuits.title: Current consumption measurement setup (SAM DA1)
circuits.description: One meter feeds VDDIN, VDDANA and VDDIO together, so it reads the whole supply current; VDDCORE, the regulator output, has only its decoupling capacitor to ground.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connection (SAM DA1)
circuits.description: A crystal between XIN and XOUT with a load capacitor CLEXT from each pin to ground; CSTRAY is the board capacitance between the two lines. The crystal is modelled as LM, CM and RM in series, shunted by CSHUNT. XOSC32K on XIN32 and XOUT32 is connected the same way.

parts.note: LM, CM and RM in series with CSHUNT across them

circuits.title: Power supply connection with filtering
circuits.description: One 1.62 V to 3.63 V rail, with 10 μF bulk to ground, feeds VDDIO and VDDIN directly, each with 100 nF at the pin. VDDANA is fed from the same rail through an inductor and has 10 μF and 100 nF to GNDANA. VDDCORE has 1 μF to ground. GNDANA and GND join the board ground.

parts.note: inductor or ferrite bead between VDD and VDDANA

notes: Low-ESR ceramic or solid tantalum capacitors.

circuits.title: Two external analog references
circuits.description: Each external reference drives its own AREF pin, AREFA on PA03 and AREFB on PA04, with 4.7 μF across the reference and 100 nF close to the pin; both return to ground.

circuits.title: One external analog reference on both AREF pins
circuits.description: A single external reference drives AREFA (PA03) and AREFB (PA04) together, with 4.7 μF across it and 100 nF close to each pin.

circuits.title: External reset circuit
circuits.description: RESET has an optional 10 kΩ pull-up to VDD and 100 nF to ground as a filter. A push-button pulls RESET to ground through 330 Ω, which limits the discharge current of the capacitor.

circuits.title: External reset circuit for EFT immunity
circuits.description: RESET has an optional 2.2 kΩ pull-up to VDD with 100 pF across it, and a push-button to ground through 330 Ω. This raises EFT immunity but does not filter slow glitches, so it does not debounce the button.

circuits.title: External clock on XIN
circuits.description: An external clock source drives XIN (PA14). XOUT (PA15) is left open or used as a GPIO.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator
circuits.description: A 0.4 MHz to 32 MHz crystal between XIN (PA14) and XOUT (PA15), each pin with a load capacitor CLEXT to ground sized with the load capacitance equation. The crystal sits as close to the part as possible.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal without load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal directly between XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01), relying on the internal load capacitance and board capacitance; suits crystals of under 12.5 pF load.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal with load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01) with a load capacitor CLEXT from each pin to ground, for better accuracy and safety factor.

circuits.title: SWCLK pull-up
circuits.description: SWCLK (PA30) is pulled up to VDD through 1 kΩ and runs on to the debugger.

circuits.title: Cortex Debug Connector (10-pin)
circuits.description: A 2 × 5 Cortex debug header: pin 1 VTref to VDD, pin 2 SWDIO to PA31, pin 4 SWDCLK to SWCLK (PA30), pin 10 nRESET to RESET, pins 3 and 5 to ground, pins 6 to 9 unconnected.

circuits.title: 10-pin JTAGICE3 compatible Serial Wire Debug header
circuits.description: A 2 × 5 header matching the JTAGICE3 50-mil cable: pin 1 SWDCLK to SWCLK (PA30), pin 2 ground, pin 4 VTG to VDD, pin 5 SWDIO to PA31, pin 6 RESET to RESET, pins 3 and 7 to 10 unconnected.

circuits.title: 20-pin IDC JTAG connector
circuits.description: A 2 × 10 IDC JTAG header used for SWD: pin 1 VCC to VDD, pin 7 SWDIO to PA31, pin 9 SWDCLK to SWCLK (PA30), pin 15 nRESET to RESET, even pins 4 to 20 to ground, the rest unconnected.
notes: Pins 14, 16, 18 and 20 (GND*) are reserved for firmware extensions; they may be left open or grounded and are not needed for SWD.

circuits.title: Low-cost USB interface
circuits.description: The USB connector's D+ and D- run as a matched differential pair to USB_D+ (PA25) and USB_D- (PA24). VBUS is brought out as a net; the connector ground and shield both go to board ground.

circuits.title: Protected USB interface
circuits.description: Five transient suppressors guard VBUS, D+ and D-: one from VBUS to the shield-side return, and on each data line one up to VBUS and one down to the return. The connector ground goes to board ground, and the shield joins it through 4.5 nF in parallel with 1 MΩ. D+ and D- run as a matched pair to USB_D+ (PA25) and USB_D- (PA24).
notes: The filter resistor reads 1MO; it is 1 MΩ.

operation.text: The SAM D21 and SAM DA1 parts share one peripheral set, one linear address map and hex-compatible code, and pin-compatible packages from 32 to 64 pins, so a design can move between members. The core reaches 2.46 CoreMark/MHz at up to 48 MHz. Every oscillator can clock the system, and separate clock domains let each peripheral run at its own rate while the CPU stays fast. Flash can be programmed in-system over SWD, which also carries non-intrusive debug; a resident bootloader may load new code over any communication interface. SERCOM blocks also cover SMBus and PMBus. The parts are drop-in compatible with the SAM D20.

Two sleep modes are selected in software. Idle halts the CPU and leaves the rest running; Standby stops all clocks and functions except those set to keep going. With SleepWalking a peripheral wakes itself on a set condition (a threshold crossed, a result ready) and only then wakes the CPU. The event system passes synchronous and asynchronous events between peripherals, Standby included.

SAM D21 runs from 1.62 V to 3.63 V and is offered to AEC-Q100 Grade 1 (-40 °C to 125 °C); SAM DA1 runs from 2.7 V to 3.63 V and is AEC-Q100 Grade 2 (-40 °C to 105 °C). Packages: 64-pin TQFP, QFN and UFBGA; 48-pin TQFP and QFN; 45- and 35-ball WLCSP; 32-pin TQFP and QFN. Up to 52 programmable I/O pins.

A SAM D21 order code reads ATSAMD 21, then pin count, Flash density, variant, a dash, package type, grade and an optional T for tape and reel. ATSAMD21G18A-MU decodes as 48 pins, 256 KB Flash, the default A variant, VQFN package, grade U (-40 °C to 85 °C, matte tin), shipped in trays. The G18A has no RWWEE section; variants B, C, D and L add it on smaller Flash sizes. L variants have no USB, I2S or PTC, carry four comparators, and offer more ADC channels than the A parts of the same pin count.

Up to five 16-bit TCs, each usable as one 16-bit or 8-bit counter with two compare/capture channels, or paired into a 32-bit counter. Up to four TCCs (24-bit, TCC2 16-bit) with up to four compare channels and complementary outputs, synchronized PWM patterns across pins, deterministic fault protection, fast decay, dead time and dithering that adds up to 5 bits of resolution; up to eight PWM channels per 24-bit TCC and two per 16-bit TCC or TC. Also a 32-bit RTC with calendar, a WDT, a CRC-32 generator, a 12-channel DMAC, a 12-channel event system, 16 external interrupts plus one NMI, and program and debug interface disable (PDID).

The ADC is 12-bit at 350 ksps with up to 20 channels, differential or single-ended inputs, a gain stage from 1/2x to 16x, automatic offset and gain error compensation, and hardware oversampling with decimation to 13, 14, 15 or 16 bits. The DAC is 10-bit at 350 ksps. Up to four comparators offer a window mode. The PTC senses touch and proximity on up to 256 channels.

One full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 interface serves as embedded host or device with eight endpoints. Up to six SERCOMs each act as a USART (full duplex or single-wire half duplex), an I2C up to 3.4 MHz, an SPI or a LIN client. One I2S interface has two channels.

Out of reset each pin is a general purpose I/O under PORT. Writing PINCFGn.PMUXEN = 1 hands the pin to a peripheral, and PMUXn.PMUXE/O picks which of functions A to H it gets. All analog functions are on B, and choosing B removes the digital control of the pin. The oscillator pins (XIN/XOUT on PA14/PA15, XIN32/XOUT32 on PA00/PA01) are switched by SYSCTRL registers, not by the PORT multiplexer.
SWCLK (PA30) is the only debug signal on the normal port functions. When a debugger is detected by cold- or hot-plugging, PA31 changes over to SWDIO without software action.

PA24 and PA25 (USB DM and DP) lack the drive-strength option. When they are not connected, enabling the pull-up with the pin as a GPIO input keeps the pad from floating and drawing extra current, below 1 mA.

The I/O pins are grouped in clusters, each fed by the supply and ground pins listed beside it; on the 48-pin package, for example, PA08 to PA11 hang off VDDIO pin 17 and GND pin 18, and the VDDANA cluster pins off VDDANA pin 6 and GNDANA pin 5.

VDDANA powers PA00 to PA07 and PB00 to PB09 together with the ADC, AC, AC1, DAC, PTC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, POR and BOD33. VDDIO powers PA08 to PA31 and PB10 to PB31 along with OSC8M and XOSC. VDDIN feeds the regulator, which holds BOD12 and whose VDDCORE output runs the digital logic (CPU and peripherals), DFLL48M and FDPLL96M.

VDDIO, VDDIN and VDDANA each accept 1.62 V to 3.63 V and must all sit at one common voltage, called VDD. VDDCORE is the 1.2 V regulated output. GND serves VDDCORE, VDDIO and VDDIN; GNDANA is the ground of VDDANA.
The regulator has a normal mode for when the CPU and peripherals run, and a low-power mode with a small quiescent current that may be used in Standby.
The POR circuit watching VDDANA needs the supply to rise at least at a minimum rate, and the rise must also stay under a maximum rate; both limits are in the electrical characteristics.

After power-up the part stays in reset until its supplies have settled. It then runs from 1 MHz: OSC8M divided by eight, fed through generic clock generator 0, which is the main clock of the Power Manager. Synchronous system clocks that are on by default run undivided at that 1 MHz; all other generic clocks are off except GCLK_WDT for the watchdog. I/O pins come up tri-stated.

When reset ends the CPU loads its stack pointer and program counter from address 0x00000000, the first location of the internal Flash. Code from Flash is then free to set up the clock system and sources.

Three monitors guard the supply. POR watches VDDANA, is always on (sleep included) and resets the whole chip when VDDANA drops below its threshold. BOD33 also watches VDDANA and is configured in SYSCTRL. BOD12 watches the internal VDDCORE once the part has started; it is calibrated in production and its settings sit in the NVM User Row, where they must be kept when that row is rewritten.

Addresses on the high-speed bus matrix are fixed and never remapped, boot included. Flash starts at 0x00000000, the RWWEE section (variants B, C, D, L) at 0x00400000, SRAM at 0x20000000, the three peripheral bridges at 0x40000000, 0x41000000 and 0x42000000, and the single-cycle IOBUS at 0x60000000. Flash is organized in 64-byte pages; the 256 KB part has 4096 pages. SRAM is single-cycle at full speed.

Calibration data sits above the main array at 0x00800000. The automatic calibration row there is copied into its registers at start-up. AUX0, the NVM User Row, starts at 0x00804000; AUX1 at 0x00806000 holds a device configuration area at 0x00806008 and a 256-bit software calibration area at 0x00806020.

The User Row, readable at 0x804000, holds power-on settings: bootloader protection size, EEPROM emulation size, BOD33 level, enable, action and hysteresis, WDT enable, always-on, period, window, early-warning offset and window enable, and the region lock bits. Its first two 32-bit words are calibration data read automatically at power-on. It is written through NVMCTRL, and new values reach the other modules only after a reset. The BOD12 bits are factory-set and must stay as they are.

Production test writes calibration values for the ADC (linearity, bias), OSC32K, the USB pads (TRANSN, TRANSP, TRIM) and the DFLL48M coarse setting into a read-only area at 0x806020. Software reads each value and copies it into the matching peripheral register.
Each device carries a 128-bit serial number made of four 32-bit words at 0x0080A00C, 0x0080A040, 0x0080A044 and 0x0080A048. It is unique only taken as all 128 bits.

The CPU is an Arm Cortex-M0+ revision r0p1 (ARMv6 architecture, Thumb-2 instruction set), instruction-compatible with the Cortex-M0 and upward compatible with the Cortex-M3 and M4. It has a 32-bit AMBA-3 AHB-Lite system port to memories and peripherals and a separate 32-bit single-cycle I/O port to PORT; because both can be used at once, instruction fetch continues during I/O access and single-cycle I/O can be sustained. Software always runs privileged; there is no MPU.

Inside the core: the System Control Space with the debug registers, the 24-bit SysTick timer clocked by CLK_CPU, the NVIC, the System Control Block for configuration and exception control, and the CoreSight MTB-M0+ trace buffer.

The NVIC offers four priority levels; each peripheral instance owns one interrupt line (lines 0 to 29, plus the EIC NMI). A peripheral raises its request when an INTFLAG bit is set and the matching bit is enabled through INTENSET (cleared through INTENCLR); all flags of one peripheral are ORed into its single line. The request sets the pending bit (ISPR/ICPR), the NVIC acts on it when enabled in ISER/ICER, and IPR0 to IPR7 hold the priorities.

The MTB records non-sequential program counter changes (branches, exception entry) as pairs of 32-bit words in SRAM, at a position and size software chooses; a debugger reads them back through the debug port to rebuild program flow. The same SRAM stays usable by the CPU, with trace writes taking priority. Tracing runs while MASTER.EN = 1; it can stop automatically at a watermark, or else the buffer wraps over old packets. Its registers (POSITION, MASTER, FLOW, BASE) start at 0x41006000, an address also listed in the CoreSight ROM table.

A symmetric crossbar with a 32-bit data path joins the hosts (CPU, DSU, DMAC data) to the clients (Flash, the three AHB-APB bridges and SRAM ports 4 to 6) at the same clock as the hosts, and lets different hosts reach different clients at the same time. The MTB, USB and the DMAC write-back and fetch channels connect straight to SRAM ports 0 to 3.

Each host reaching SRAM carries a QoS level from 0 (background) to 3 (critical latency). Concurrent accesses are ordered first by QoS and then by port number, lowest port first. Levels 0 and 1 add at least one cycle of latency. The MTB is fixed at level 3 and the DSU at level 1; the CPU level sits in bits [1:0] at 0x41007120 and resets to 0x2. USB and DMAC set theirs in their own QOSCTRL registers.

Each bridge is an AHB client giving access to peripheral control registers on the low-power APB side. It follows the AMBA APB v2.0 (APB4) protocol with wait states, error reporting, transaction protection and byte/half-word/word sparse transfers, merges the address and data cycles into one, and applies sparse transfer to reads as well. CLK_HPBx_AHB must be running.

Each bridge has a PAC that can write-protect the registers of the peripherals on it. CLK_PAC0_APB and CLK_PAC1_APB are on after reset; CLK_PAC2_APB is off. The PAC works in any sleep mode whose clock keeps running. A write to a protected peripheral is dropped and raises an access error (CPU exception); debugger writes ignore protection. Protection is set through WPSET and cleared through WPCLR, both reading the same value, so no read-modify-write is needed. Protecting an already protected peripheral, or unprotecting an unprotected one, also raises an error, which can catch a broken program flow; code that changes protection from interrupts should read WPSET first.

PAC registers accept 8-, 16- and 32-bit atomic access, and the bytes and half-words of a register can be reached directly. Touching a register that is write-protected, enable-protected or busy synchronizing is illegal and ends in a hard fault.

The Device Service Unit detects a debug probe, gives the Arm Debug Access Port control over the debug pads and CPU reset, holds the CoreSight ROM that identifies the device and its debug components, and offers memory services (CRC32, MBIST) such as IEC 60730 Class B testing needs. It sits on the bus matrix, so the CPU and a debugger can use it at once. When the NVMCTRL security bit is set, some of its services are restricted or unavailable.

At reset SWCLK belongs to the DSU for probe detection and reset stretching. If the PORT gives SWCLK another function or the PORT multiplexer is turned off, hot-plugging stays disabled until a power or external reset. The DSU keeps running in Idle. CLK_DSU_APB and CLK_DSU_AHB are gated in the Power Manager. It uses no DMA, interrupts or events. Its writable registers can be PAC-protected, apart from DCC0 and DCC1, and protection never applies to an external debugger.

If SWCLK is low when RESET is released, the DSU keeps the CPU in reset after the rest of the system starts, so a debugger can connect before any code runs. SWCLK is pulled up internally at start-up so a floating pin is not taken for a debugger. STATUSA.CRSTEXT reads 1 while the CPU is held; writing 1 to it releases the CPU. On a protected device the release is refused and STATUSA.PERR is set.

Cold-plugging is detection while in reset, through the reset extension. Hot-plugging is detection while running, on a falling edge of SWCLK; it cannot happen during POR or RESET, needs SWCLK left on its debug function, is reported in STATUSB.HPE, and is unavailable on a protected device. Either detection sets STATUSB.DBGPRES. The pads must be powered, so detection waits for POR release; on a protected device only cold-plugging works, so the external reset must last longer than POR, and the attempt is repeated if RESET was released before POR.

Chip-Erase wipes volatile memories, the whole Flash with its EEPROM emulation area, plus the RWWEE section, and clears the security bit; the auxiliary rows, User Row included, are kept. It starts by writing 1 to CTRL.CE (ignored if the DSU is PAC-protected) and ends when STATUSA.DONE reads 1. On a protected device the debugger must reset it first to be detected. The usual sequence: cold-plug so the CPU is held, write CTRL.CE, poll STATUSA.DONE, then reset so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Programming needs an unprotected device. The debugger holds RESET low through power-up while the regulator keeps the part in POR until the supply passes its threshold and the internal rails are safe; the PM then starts on the slow clock. Holding SWCLK low, the debugger releases RESET (cold-plug), clocks SWCLK to wake the DAP, issues a Chip-Erase and programs through the AHB-AP while the CPU stays in reset. Afterwards it restarts the part by RESET or a power cycle, with SWCLK high as RESET rises so the CPU is not held.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit stops external tools reaching the internal memories; only a Chip-Erase removes it. On a protected device AHB-AP accesses outside the DSU external range are discarded by the DSU security filter and set the AHB-AP sticky error bits. The CPU reaches the DSU without limits. The DSU registers at 0x0000-0x00FF are mirrored at 0x0100-0x01FF: the first copy is the internal range (closed to debug tools when protected), the second the external range, and the CoreSight ROM sits at 0x1000-0x1FFF. A protected device accepts MEM-AP accesses only in 0x0100-0x2000.

Once PDID is activated, only code running on the part can write the Flash. Chip-Erase and reprogramming through the debug port fail, and so does every read-out of Flash, RAM or other content. Microchip publishes a SAMD21 PDID library.

Identification follows the Arm CoreSight scheme. The ROM table address is in the MEM-AP BASE register of the DAP, and PID0 to PID7 form a 64-bit conceptual ID: JEP-106 code 0x1F with continuation 0x0, part number 0xCD0 (a DSU is present). With REVISION 0x0 the device is then fully identified from the DSU DID register, which gives processor, product family, product series and device select.

CRC32 and MBIST share the ADDR, LENGTH and DATA registers: load them, then start a command through CTRL. Further commands are ignored until STATUSA.DONE is set. Turning on its clocks enables it. Debug adapters use the external range 0x100-0x2000 (the first 0x100 bytes return an error on a protected device); the CPU should use the internal range 0x0-0x100.

The DSU computes the standard CRC32 (polynomial 0xEDB88320, reversed form) over any memory the bus matrix reaches, Flash and AHB RAM included. ADDR takes the word-aligned start, LENGTH the word-aligned size, DATA the seed (normally 0xFFFFFFFF, or a previous result to chain blocks); writing CTRL.CRC = 1 starts it and CTRL.SWRST aborts it. When STATUSA.DONE sets, check STATUSA.BERR, then read DATA; complement it to match common CRC32 results, or keep it raw to chain. From the external range the area and seed are forced (full array or full EEPROM emulation area, seed 0xFFFFFFFF).

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake that both CPU and debugger can use, even on a protected device, to pass data at run time or in debug and build a custom debug protocol. STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D flag a new write and clear when read. On a protected device a debugger cannot attach while the CPU runs. The channels share hardware with MBIST and must not be used during an MBIST run.

The memory built-in self test, meant mainly for production, runs a March LR algorithm in time linear with memory size: write all zeros; read 0/write 1 descending; read 1/write 0/read 0/write 1 ascending; read 1/write 0 ascending; read 0/write 1/read 1/write 0 ascending; read all zeros. It finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling and linked coupling faults. Run time depends on CPU clock and RAM size tested. Load ADDR and LENGTH (a whole physical block gives the best coverage), then write CTRL.MBIST = 1; CTRL.SWRST cancels. With ADDR.AMOD = 0 the test exits on the first fault, setting STATUSA.DONE and STATUSA.FAIL; with AMOD = 1 it pauses with STATUSA.FAIL set until FAIL is written 1. ADDR then holds the failing word's address and DATA the phase and bit index. MBIST from the external range on a protected device sets STATUSA.PERR instead.

External access means DSU offsets 0x200-0x1FFF; internal access means offsets 0x000-0x100. From the external range of a protected device Chip-Erase, CRC32 (full array or full RWWEE only), CoreSight identification and the debug channels remain; MBIST and clearing STATUSA.CRSTEXT do not.

Three blocks make the clocks. SYSCTRL runs the sources: XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. GCLK turns them into generic clocks: each generator is a prescaler that may take any source, and each generic clock multiplexer picks a generator and gates the result to one peripheral (several instances of a peripheral usually have one generic clock each). Generator 0 drives GCLK_MAIN, from which the PM makes the synchronous CPU, AHB and APB clocks, with prescalers and a mask bit per peripheral bus interface. Generic clock 0 is the DFLL48M reference when the DFLL multiplies another clock. SERCOM0, for instance, can run from the DFLL48M in open loop through generator 1 and generic clock 20 (GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE), with CLK_SERCOM0_APB unmasked in the PM APBC mask.

Synchronous clocks are the CPU and bus clocks; asynchronous clocks are the generic clocks from GCLK. A peripheral whose core runs on a generic clock needs CPU accesses to some of its registers carried across the clock boundary, in hardware, even when both clocks come from the same source at the same frequency. Bus-interface registers need no synchronization; core registers are synchronized on write and some on read.

The GCLK, WDT, RTC, EIC, TC, ADC, DAC and AC each use one synchronizer for all of a peripheral's core registers, flagged by STATUS.SYNCBUSY. While a write is being synchronized, writing a core register, reading a read-synchronized register or reading the register being written stalls the bus until it ends; core registers without read synchronization and APB registers read without stalling. Reading a read-synchronized register always stalls the bus at once (without setting SYNCBUSY), and stalls twice if a write synchronization is already running. Completion is seen by polling SYNCBUSY, by the synchronization-ready interrupt where one exists, or by simply issuing the next access, which waits.

Peripherals with a READREQ register can fetch a read-synchronized value without stalling the bus. Writing READREQ.RREQ = 1 with the register's offset in READREQ.ADDR starts one synchronization (SYNCBUSY set until done); the value then reads without delay until RREQ is written again. READREQ.RCONT = 1 (with RREQ set once) keeps the chosen register continuously synchronized, so the latest value is always readable; SYNCBUSY is set only for the first pass. A write to a write-synchronized register stops a continuous request, which must then be restarted. Continuous synchronization pauses in sleep modes where the generic clock stops, so a fresh request is needed for a value right after wake-up.

Writing CTRL.ENABLE starts a write synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY; ENABLE reads back its new value at once. Writing CTRL.SWRST = 1 does the same; SWRST reads 1 at once and SWRST and SYNCBUSY clear when the reset is done; writing 0 does nothing. During either, writing a core or APB register or reading a read-synchronized register stalls the bus; APB reads do not. The synchronization-ready interrupt cannot signal either of these.

SERCOM USART, SPI and I2C, I2S, TCC and USB synchronize each register on its own, with one bit per register in SYNCBUSY. Registers synchronize in parallel; a second write to a register whose previous write is still synchronizing is discarded and reported as an error (for example a 16-bit register written as two back-to-back byte writes). Read-synchronized registers are synchronized whenever their value changes and read back immediately. The synchronization-ready flag sets when every SYNCBUSY bit is 0. CTRL.ENABLE and CTRLA.SWRST set SYNCBUSY.ENABLE and SYNCBUSY.SWRST and clear them when done.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs a running clock source, an enabled generator using that source, its generic clock multiplexer set to that generator and enabled, and its bus interface unmasked in the PM; while masked, its registers read 0 and writes are lost. When a peripheral is disabled while pins it drives have a pin-change interrupt enabled, a wake-up can occur without its interrupt flag set, leaving the wake source unknown; clearing the peripheral's interrupt enables (or its NVIC enable) before disabling it prevents this.

Every clock source can run on demand: it stays stopped until a peripheral asks for it. The request passes from the peripheral through its generic clock and generator to the source, and only if all three are enabled; the source starts or keeps running while any request is active and stops when the last one ends. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it running regardless, removing its start-up time at the cost of current. Setting the RUNSTDBY bits along the path lets requests work in standby.
A slower peripheral clock lowers that peripheral's active current but lengthens synchronization with the CPU clock domain, so response is slower.

Any reset returns the synchronous clocks to OSC8M enabled with a divide-by-8 prescaler, generator 0 on OSC8M producing GCLK_MAIN, and CPU and bus clocks undivided. A power reset also returns GCLK to its initial state: every generator off except generator 0 (OSC8M, undivided, GCLK_MAIN) and generator 2 (OSCULP32K, undivided), and every generic clock off except the WDT's, fed by generator 2. A user reset does the same except for generic clocks locked by WRTLOCK, the WDT generic clock when the NVM User Row sets WDT always-on at power-up, and the RTC's generic clock when it is enabled. Clock sources return to their initial state on any reset, except the 32 kHz sources, which only a power reset resets.

The generic clock controller has nine generators that take internal or external sources and divide them; their outputs feed generic clock multiplexers, one per peripheral clock (GCLK_PERIPHERAL), so the number of multiplexers follows the peripherals present. Generator 0 always drives GCLK_MAIN. A generator's source can be changed while it runs.

GCLK_IO lines need their pins set up in PORT. GCLK can run in sleep modes. Its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is masked in the PM. GCLK has no DMA, interrupt, event or debug connections. The PAC can write-protect its writable registers, a protection that does not apply to an external debugger.

Enable the clock source first. Then: one 32-bit write to GENDIV giving the generator (ID) and division (DIV); one 32-bit write to GENCTRL giving the generator (ID), its source and GENEN = 1; one 16-bit write to CLKCTRL giving the generic clock (ID) and the generator it uses (GEN). GENCTRL, GENDIV and CLKCTRL are reached indirectly: to read one, write the wanted ID (an 8-bit write to the ID field) and then read the register. GCLK has no module enable; CTRL.SWRST resets every register except generic clocks and their generators locked with CLKCTRL.WRTLOCK.

Each generator runs from one of eight sources; generator 1 has seven, as it may not feed itself. Generator 1 is the only generator that can serve as the source of the other generators. Generator x pairs with pin GCLK_IO[x], which can be its clock input or show its output. Each generator divides its source, is enabled on its own with GENCTRL.GENEN (disabled, its output is gated), and may feed one or more generic clocks. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN for the PM.

Writing GENCTRL.SRC switches the source on the fly: the generator keeps running on the old source until the new one is ready, holding requests to both, then switches and drops the old request. Before moving generator 0 from one source to another, set ONDEMAND on the old source so the change completes properly.
GENDIV.DIV sets the division; GENCTRL.DIVSEL chooses how it is read (the field width differs per generator). An odd division gives an uneven duty cycle unless GENCTRL.IDC = 1, which makes it 50/50.

With GENCTRL.OE = 1 and GENEN = 1 the generator requests its source and drives its clock on GCLK_IO. With OE = 0 the pin holds GENCTRL.OOV: low when OOV = 0, high when OOV = 1, while the generator is off. In standby an output clock freezes at OOV unless GENCTRL.RUNSTDBY = 1, which keeps it running.

Select a generator with CLKCTRL.GEN, then set CLKCTRL.CLKEN = 1; CLKEN is synchronized to the generic clock domain and reads its old value until done. Writing CLKEN = 0 gates the clock once synchronized. To change a generic clock's generator without a glitch: write CLKEN = 0, wait until it reads 0, write the new GEN, then write CLKEN = 1.

Setting CLKCTRL.WRTLOCK makes a generic clock ignore further CLKCTRL writes and also locks the GENCTRL and GENDIV of its generator; only a power reset unlocks them, not CTRL.SWRST. Generator 0 cannot be locked, being GCLK_MAIN: any reset returns it to its known configuration. Some generators and generic clocks are on after reset so that certain peripherals have a clock; the reset values of GENCTRL, GENDIV and CLKCTRL depend on their ID.

When sleep has stopped the generic clocks, any peripheral wanting its clock for a task asks GCLK, which wakes the source, enables the generator and generic clock in turn and delivers the clock (SleepWalking). In standby a generator can keep driving GCLK_IO.

GENCTRL, GENDIV and CTRL are write-synchronized. STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done; an access needing synchronization while it is set stalls the bus (and the CPU, with interrupts pending) until it completes.

The power manager handles reset, synchronous clock generation and sleep. From GCLK_MAIN it makes the CPU and AHB clock and one clock per APB bridge, each with its own division, changeable at run time, and it masks the clock of each module. Before standby, enough clocks and peripherals must be turned off that the regulator, in its low-power mode during standby, is not overloaded. Interrupts from enabled peripherals and enabled reset sources wake the device. Its reset controller gathers every reset source and records which one acted.

Power reset sources: POR, BOD12, BOD33. User reset sources: the RESET pin, the watchdog, and software reset. A reset cause register. CPU, AHB and APB clocks from GCLK_MAIN with prescaling from 1x to 128x, safe run-time clock switching, and a clock mask per module. Sleep modes IDLE and STANDBY, with SleepWalking on GCLK clocks.

CLK_PM_APB can be masked in the PM itself; once masked, only a reset turns it back on. CLK_MAIN, from GCLK_MAIN, feeds one 8-bit prescaler for the CPU, AHB and APB clocks. Stopping CLK_CPU stops instruction execution. CLK_AHB is always at the CPU frequency and in step with it but can run with the CPU clock stopped; each AHB peripheral clock has its own gate. Each APBx clock is in step with the CPU clock, can be divided, keeps running with the CPU clock stopped, and gates each module on its bus.

The PM interrupt line goes to the NVIC. With the CPU halted by a debugger the PM runs normally, and in sleep its clocks are kept running so the debugger can reach every module, so current cannot be measured in debug. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG and RCAUSE; protection does not apply to an external debugger.

The POR detector holds the device in reset until the supply is stable, so no external reset circuit is needed at power-up. After POR, RCAUSE.POR is set, the default GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, the main clock is GCLK_MAIN undivided, the device is in active mode and only the peripheral clocks that are enabled by default run. The PM is always enabled and cannot be reset. Active mode has every clock domain running.

Each synchronous clock can take any tap of the 8-bit prescaler or the undivided main clock, provided fCPU ≥ fAPBx and no domain exceeds its maximum frequency. CPUSEL.CPUDIV divides the CPU (and AHB) clock and APBxSEL.APBxDIV each APB clock. They can be written without stopping peripherals, together or one at a time, so the CPU can be rescaled with the APB frequency held. After a write the new setting takes a moment to apply; INTFLAG.CKRDY reads 0 meanwhile and can raise the PM interrupt when it is ready. Rewriting CPUSEL while CKRDY is 0 can leave the system unstable or hung.

Writing a module's bit in AHBMASK or APBxMASK to 0 or 1 stops or starts its bus clock; with its APB clock stopped a module's registers can be neither read nor written. A module on several clock domains has several mask bits. Masking NVMCTRL breaks CPU reads of Flash; masking the PM or its APB bridge makes the mask registers unwritable until a system reset.

RCAUSE holds the last reset cause. Power resets (POR, BOD12, BOD33) come from SYSCTRL and are electrical; user resets are the RESET pin, the watchdog and SysResetReq, the CPU's software reset set through SYSRESETREQ in its reset control register. Pulling RESET low resets the device; the pin has an internal pull-up and needs no drive in normal operation.

WFI enters sleep; SLEEP.IDLE and the CPU's SCR.SLEEPDEEP bit choose the mode. In IDLE the CPU stops and, by the IDLE level, some synchronous clock domains stop too, whatever the PM mask bits say; the regulator stays in normal mode and wake-up is fastest. IDLE is entered by WFI with SCR.SLEEPDEEP = 0 and SLEEP.IDLE set, or, with SCR.SLEEPONEXIT set, on return from the lowest-priority interrupt handler; any interrupt not masked in the NVIC and of enough priority returns the device to active. In STANDBY every clock stops except those requested by a running module or with ONDEMAND = 0 (the RTC can run, keeping its generic clock source on); regulator and RAM go to low-power mode and RAM keeps its contents. STANDBY is entered by WFI with SCR.SLEEPDEEP = 1 and SLEEPONEXIT also works; any peripheral able to raise an asynchronous interrupt wakes it, and the CPU then runs the handler or carries on according to PRIMASK.

In STANDBY a peripheral can have its clock started for a task without waking the CPU; afterwards it either wakes the device with an interrupt or the device stays in STANDBY. On this device SleepWalking works only for GCLK clocks, through the on-demand clock requests.

The PM has one interrupt source, clock ready (CKRDY). A flag in INTFLAG sets on its condition, INTENSET and INTENCLR enable and disable it by writing 1, and the request holds until software writes 1 to the flag, disables the interrupt or resets the module; with one shared line, INTFLAG tells which source fired. In the IDLE modes the PM keeps running on the main clock; in STANDBY it is frozen and returns to active on any asynchronous interrupt.

SYSCTRL is the control interface of the clock sources, the brown-out detectors, the internal regulator and the voltage reference: it enables, disables, calibrates and monitors them. PCLKSR collects every status bit, and each can raise an interrupt through INTENSET, INTENCLR and INTFLAG. A BOD33 interrupt can wake the device from standby.

XOSC: 0.4-32 MHz crystal oscillator with adjustable gain, selectable start-up time, crystal or external clock on XIN. XOSC32K: 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator with automatic or manual gain, selectable start-up, crystal or external clock on XIN32. OSC32K: 32.768 kHz high-accuracy internal oscillator with fine tuning and selectable start-up. OSCULP32K: 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power internal oscillator, always on, fine tuning, calibration loaded from factory Flash at reset. OSC8M: quick-starting 8 MHz internal oscillator, fine tuning, divided outputs of 4, 2 and 1 MHz, calibration from factory Flash at reset. DFLL48M: 48 MHz internal oscillator with no external parts, an adjustable oscillator in open loop or a multiplier of a known clock in closed loop. FDPLL96M: 48-96 MHz output from a 32 kHz-2 MHz reference, three reference choices, adjustable PI controller, fractional part giving steps of 1/16 of the reference. BOD33: programmable threshold, low-power sampled mode, threshold from Flash user calibration at start-up, reset or interrupt, hysteresis. VREG: normal and low-power modes, with a fixed internal BOD12. VREF: bandgap with programmable calibration (loaded from factory Flash at start-up) and a temperature sensor.

SYSCTRL sets up the XOSC and XOSC32K pins itself when they are enabled. It keeps working in sleep as long as the clock it uses runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events can act without waking it. It supplies XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M to GCLK. Its bus clock is CLK_SYSCTRL_APB. The BOD33 sampling clock and the DFLL48M control logic (run from the DFLL output) are asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register writes are synchronized. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. SYSCTRL keeps running with the CPU halted by a debugger. When the device detects a debugger cold-plug, the BOD33 reset is masked (BOD resets stay active on hot-plug), so a BOD33 level set too high for the supply can be corrected. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG.

A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 and a 0.4-32 MHz crystal between XIN and XOUT, each with the load capacitors it needs; recommended crystal parameters and load capacitance are in the electrical characteristics.

Each oscillator runs only with ENABLE = 1 in its control register. PCLKSR status bits can raise interrupts and, for some, wake the device from standby. By default an oscillator runs in idle only when a peripheral requests it (ONDEMAND resets to 1) and stops in standby. ONDEMAND = 0 keeps it running in idle; RUNSTDBY = 1 lets it run in standby on request, and with ONDEMAND = 0 as well it runs in standby always. OSCULP32K always runs and cannot be disabled.

XOSC takes an external clock on XIN or drives a 0.4-32 MHz crystal, and can source any generator. It is off after reset, leaving XIN and XOUT free as GPIO or for other peripherals. XOSC.ENABLE = 1 turns it on; XOSC.XTALEN = 1 selects crystal mode, where SYSCTRL takes both pins, and XTALEN = 0 selects external clock, where only XIN is taken and XOUT stays usable as GPIO. In crystal mode XOSC.GAIN must match the crystal frequency; XOSC.AMPGC = 1 adjusts the amplitude automatically, usually for less current. After a hard reset or a wake-up from a sleep mode where it was off, the output is masked for the start-up time chosen in XOSC.STARTUP, after which PCLKSR.XOSCRDY sets (with an interrupt on its rising edge if INTENSET.XOSCRDY is set). Standby must not be entered while any oscillator is starting: wait for its ready bit in PCLKSR.

XOSC32K takes an external clock on XIN32 or drives a 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 and XOUT32, and can source any generator. It is off after POR with both pins free. XOSC32K.ENABLE = 1 turns it on; XTALEN = 1 selects crystal mode (both pins taken), XTALEN = 0 external clock (only XIN32 taken, XOUT32 still GPIO). Disable it by writing ENABLE = 0 with the other bits unchanged: writing ENABLE together with other bits can behave unpredictably. Once enabled it stays on in every sleep mode. XOSC32K.STARTUP sets the masked start-up time; PCLKSR.XOSC32KRDY then sets, with an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSC32KRDY is set. Because a 32 kHz crystal can take up to one second to start, XOSC32K keeps running through every reset except POR. With a crystal, XOSC32K.EN32K = 1 enables its 32.768 kHz output; EN32K does not work with an external clock on XIN32. Standby must not be entered while it is starting.

OSC32K is a tunable low-power 32 kHz source for the generators, off by default. It starts only with both OSC32K.ENABLE and OSC32K.EN32K (its 32.768 kHz output) set; PCLKSR.OSC32KRDY goes high when it is stable. Its frequency is set by OSC32K.CALIB, which software must write, using the factory value kept in the NVM software calibration area; a new CALIB takes effect once OSC32KRDY is high.

OSCULP32K is a tunable ultra-low-power 32 kHz source, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, the choice over OSC32K when current matters more than frequency stability and accuracy. It is on after POR and runs at all times except during POR, with a 32.768 kHz and a 1.024 kHz output always running. OSCULP32K.CALIB loads from factory Flash at start-up to correct for process and can be overwritten.

OSC8M is an open-loop 8 MHz internal oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, and the default clock after POR. OSC8M.ENABLE turns it on and off. OSC8M.CALIB loads from factory Flash at start-up to correct for process; OSC8M.FRANGE and CALIB can be rewritten to change the frequency, best not while it is enabled. Being open loop, its frequency moves with voltage, temperature and process. It stops automatically in some sleep modes.

The DFLL48M runs open loop or closed loop and can source any generator; in closed loop an accurate low-frequency reference gives an accurate output, CLK_DFLL48M. Every reset selects open loop, where DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE set the frequency; loading the DFLL48M COARSE CAL value from the NVM software calibration area into COARSE gives close to 48 MHz. COARSE and FINE can be changed while the DFLL runs and is in use. The output is ready once PCLKSR.DFLLRDY sets after enable.

In closed loop the output is held continuously against a reference, with fine tuning automatic once the multiplier is set. After enabling the DFLL: enable and select the reference, generic clock channel 0 (GCLK_DFLL48M_REF); set the largest coarse and fine steps in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and DFLLMUL.FSTEP, no more than half the largest COARSE and FINE values (small steps give little overshoot and slower lock, large steps the reverse); set DFLLMUL.MUL so the output stays under the DFLL's maximum; then write DFLLCTRL.MODE = 1. In closed loop COARSE and FINE are read-only and driven by the tuner, which starts from the COARSE value written beforehand: a value near the final one shortens coarse lock. Loading DFLL48M COARSE CAL into COARSE, setting DFLLCTRL.BPLCKC and then starting closed loop cuts the lock time down to the fine lock time.

Closed-loop lock has two stages: a fast coarse search of DFLLVAL.COARSE that brings the output near the target and sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKC, then fine tuning of DFLLVAL.FINE that sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKF. Each lock bit can raise an interrupt. The clock is usable once PCLKSR.DFLLRDY is set, with an accuracy that depends on which locks are held; lock times are in the electrical characteristics.

With DFLLCTRL.STABLE = 0 the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement. An unstable or drifting reference can push FINE past its limits, setting PCLKSR.DFLLOOB; the closed-loop reference must be stable: an external oscillator, preferably XOSC32K, and never an internal oscillator. If the reference stops or falls below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MULMAX), PCLKSR.DFLLRCS sets (with an interrupt if enabled); detection can take about 2^17 CLK_DFLL48M cycles. The DFLL then runs as in open loop and returns to closed loop by itself when the reference comes back.

operation.topic: DFLL48M chill cycles and quick lock
operation.text: A newly selected frequency can take several microseconds to appear at the output, which with a small MUL can upset locking. Chill cycles skip a measurement to allow for this; they are on by default, may double the lock time, and are turned off with DFLLCTRL.CCDIS = 1. Quick lock relaxes the lock criteria, is also on by default, and is turned off with DFLLCTRL.QLDIS = 1; its output frequency varies more than with chill cycles, with the same average.

Setting DFLLCTRL.USBCRM and DFLLCTRL.MODE makes the DFLL lock to the USB start-of-frame, which a connected device receives every 1 ms, in place of the generic clock reference; a multiplier of 0xBB80 then gives 48 MHz. In this mode the DFLL status bits follow bus activity and mean nothing, BPLCKC is ignored, the COARSE value written (from the NVM calibration row) is used as the final coarse value, and locking goes straight to the fine search. Clear DFLLCTRL.QLDIS and set CCDIS for a faster lock; STABLE is ignored and an automatic jitter reduction is used.

operation.topic: DFLL48M wake from sleep and accuracy
operation.text: With DFLLCTRL.LLAW = 0 a DFLL that was disabled restarts with its previous settings and keeps its locks even without the reference; once the reference returns, fine tracking corrects drift during sleep if STABLE = 0. With LLAW = 1 it loses its locks when turned off and goes through the whole lock sequence again. Accuracy at fine lock depends on the fine step (smaller at higher output frequency), on the measurement resolution (a small output-to-reference ratio can lock below target; a reference of 32 kHz or less avoids this at low target frequencies) and on the reference's own accuracy.

The FDPLL96M is a digital PLL made of a time-to-digital converter, a PI digital filter, a digitally controlled oscillator and a lock controller, multiplying its reference by a fractional ratio. The reference CLK_FDPLL96M_REF is XOSC32K, XOSC (through a divider) or GCLK_DPLL; it must be set up and running first, and within the input range (XOSC divided by the chosen divider, or GCLK_DPLL's source). The internal lock timer needs a 32 kHz generic clock, GCLK_DPLL_32K. The output CLK_FDPLL96M is controlled only by the PLL's own output clock gate. Disabling the PLL resets its output. With DPLLRATIO.LDRFRAC = 0 it runs in integer mode, otherwise in fractional mode, which adds jitter. For a 32 kHz reference, 48 MHz needs a ratio of 1500 (LDR = 1499); 48.006 MHz needs 1500.1875 (LDR = 1499, LDRFRAC = 3).

DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE turns the PLL on and off. The output is stable once enabled and DPLLSTATUS.LOCK is set. With DPLLCTRLB.LTIME not 0, lock is declared after that fixed time; with LTIME = 0 lock follows the PLL's status and the time depends on the filter and target frequency. DPLLCTRLB.WUF = 1 (wake-up fast) opens the output gate at the end of start-up, before the frequency has settled, saving several milliseconds. After the first acquisition, DPLLCTRLB.LBYPASS chooses whether loss of lock gates the output. To change reference: disable the PLL, change DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK, enable it again. DPLLRATIO may be rewritten while it runs: LOCK clears and sets again when the output settles, and the lock-lost flag INTFLAG.DPLLLCK sets on a falling lock edge, cleared by writing 1. The PI filter adjusts itself for stability against jitter; DPLLCTRLB.FILTER overrides it and DPLLCTRLB.LPEN bypasses the TDC.

BOD33 watches VDDANA against the threshold in BOD33.LEVEL and gives an interrupt or a reset when the supply falls below it; PCLKSR.BOD33DET shows the state. Level, action, hysteresis and enable load from the NVM User Row at start-up and POR and can be overwritten. Continuous mode (BOD33.MODE = 0, the default) watches all the time. Sampled mode (MODE = 1) turns the detector on briefly at each tick of a sampling clock and leaves it off between; it then asks for its reference only when needed, and that reference is ready from 95 % of its target voltage, so the threshold can shift by up to 5 % when nothing else holds the bandgap on in standby (regulator not in LDO mode with VREG.RUNSTDBY = 0, ADC, AC and DAC not using the bandgap, AC voltage doubler off). The sampling clock is a 1 kHz output of OSCULP32K divided by BOD33.PSEL. The sampling domain is synchronized: writes to BOD33 are ignored while PCLKSR.B33SRDY is 0. Clear BOD33.CEN before changing the prescaler; in sampled mode wait for B33SRDY, then write PSEL. BOD33.HYST = 1 adds hysteresis in either mode.

VREF holds a bandgap reference, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature with VREF.CAL loaded from factory Flash at reset, and a temperature sensor whose output voltage is linear in temperature over CMIN to CMAX (the voltage and range are in the electrical characteristics). VREF.TSEN = 1 turns the sensor on; it can be routed to the ADC and is absent on DA1 devices. VREF.BGOUTEN = 1 routes the bandgap to the ADC. VREF.CALIB sets the bandgap level and can be overwritten. The internal regulator VREG supplies the core logic, VDDCORE.

The DFLL48M control registers live in another clock domain. Before writing any of them, PCLKSR.DFLLRDY must be 1; writes while it is 0 are ignored. To read them, write DFLLSYNC.READREQ = 1 and read once DFLLRDY is set; a read without it starts a synchronization and holds the bus until done. Reads with the DFLL disabled do not hold the bus. The BOD33 sampling prescaler is also asynchronous: a write to the BOD33 register starts a synchronization flagged by PCLKSR.B33SRDY, during which writing BOD33 or reading it back stalls the bus; poll B33SRDY, use its interrupt, or just issue the next access.

The watchdog resets the system if software does not clear it within its time-out, recovering from runaway or stuck code; an early-warning interrupt can come before the time-out. Window mode also resets on a clear that comes too early, which catches code that clears it too often. Once enabled it runs in active and every sleep mode from its own clock, independent of the CPU, so it still resets or interrupts if the main clocks fail. Time-outs run from 8 to 16,000 clock cycles in normal mode and 16 to 32,000 in window mode, and it can be made always-on.

The WDT works in any sleep mode where its clock runs, and its interrupt can wake the device. CLK_WDT_APB is on by default. GCLK_WDT must be set up in GCLK first and is asynchronous to the bus, so some registers synchronize. GCLK_WDT is meant to come from OSCULP32K, whose low accuracy makes the real time-out differ between devices; time-outs must allow for that spread. A more accurate source can be used at more current. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC; the WDT has no events. It halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG.

CTRL.WEN, CTRL.ALWAYSON, CONFIG and EWCTRL are enable-protected: writes while the WDT is enabled or being enabled are lost, and writes during disabling complete once it is off. Configure with the WDT off: CONFIG.PER for the time-out; for window mode also CONFIG.WINDOW and CTRL.WEN = 1; for the early warning EWCTRL.EWOFFSET and INTENSET.EW = 1. After a power-on reset CTRL.ENABLE, CTRL.ALWAYSON, CTRL.WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW, CONFIG.PER and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET load from the NVM User Row. CTRL.ENABLE starts and stops it; it can be stopped only while ALWAYSON is 0.

Once enabled, the WDT resets the system at the end of the CONFIG.PER period unless cleared before then. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR restarts the period; writing any other value resets the system at once. There are 12 time-out periods (TOWDT) from 8 ms to 16 s. The early warning is off by default; INTENSET.EW turns it on and INTENCLR.EW off. In normal mode EWCTRL.EWOFFSET sets how many GCLK_WDT cycles after the period starts it fires: with CONFIG.PER = 0x2 and EWOFFSET = 0x1 the warning comes after 16 cycles and the reset after 32. An offset longer than the period means the reset comes first and the warning never does.

In window mode the WDT has a closed window (TOWDTW, set by CONFIG.WINDOW) followed by an open window (TOWDT, set by CONFIG.PER), each 8 ms to 16 s, so the whole time-out is their sum. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR is accepted only in the open window; a clear in the closed window resets the system. The early warning, if enabled, fires as the open window starts, which a sleeping system can use to wake, clear the WDT and go on or sleep again.

Setting CTRL.ALWAYSON keeps the WDT running whatever CTRL.ENABLE says; only a power-on reset clears it. CONFIG and EWCTRL become read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed, but CTRL.WEN may still switch window mode and the early-warning interrupt may still be enabled or disabled. Software must never set ALWAYSON while GCLK_WDT, its generator or that generator's source is off.

The one interrupt source is the early warning (EW), on one shared request line. CTRL and CLEAR are write-synchronized: STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done, and an access needing synchronization while it is set stalls the bus and the CPU, with interrupts pending, until it completes.

The RTC is a 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit prescaler, normally left running to keep time. It can wake the device by alarm/compare match, periodic event or overflow. Its clock GCLK_RTC comes from GCLK and is divided by the prescaler to the resolution wanted. It makes periodic events from the prescaler taps, alarm/compare interrupts and events at any count, and overflow interrupts and events, and can clear itself on a match for long, accurate periodic intervals. From 32.768 kHz the shortest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out is over 136 years.

32-bit counter with 10-bit prescaler; several clock sources; a counter mode of 32 bits with one compare value or of 16 bits with two; a calendar mode keeping seconds, minutes and hours (12 or 24 hour), day, month and year, and leap-year correction; digital correction of the prescaler for accuracy; overflow, alarm/compare and prescaler interrupts and events, with optional clear on match.

The RTC keeps running in any sleep mode where its clock runs; its interrupts wake the device and its events act without waking it. Only power-on reset and CTRL.SWRST reset it. CLK_RTC_APB is masked in the PM. GCLK_RTC must be set up in GCLK first and is asynchronous to the bus, so some registers synchronize; the RTC should not use generator 0. Its events go to the event system and its interrupt to the NVIC. It halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL makes it run on. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, READREQ, STATUS and DBGCTRL. A 32.768 kHz crystal with its load capacitors can be fitted on XIN32 and XOUT32.

Modes: 0, COUNT32, a 32-bit counter; 1, COUNT16, a 16-bit counter; 2, CLOCK, a clock/calendar with alarm. CTRL.MODE, CTRL.PRESCALER, CTRL.MATCHCLR, CTRL.CLKREP and EVCTRL are enable-protected: writes while enabled or being enabled are lost, and writes during disabling complete once it is off. Before enabling, set the mode, the clock representation and the prescaler. In clock/calendar mode the counter must receive 1 Hz. CTRL.ENABLE starts and stops it. CTRL.SWRST resets every register but DEBUG and disables it; disable the RTC before resetting it.

With CTRL.MODE = 0 the counter counts up on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT to 0xFFFFFFFF, wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 32 bits. A match with COMP0 sets INTFLAG.CMP0 on the next CLK_RTC_CNT rising edge. With CTRL.MATCHCLR = 1 the counter clears on the cycle after a COMP0 match, giving periods longer than the prescaler events allow; CMP0 and OVF then set together.

With CTRL.MODE = 1 the counter counts up to the value in PER, wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 16 bits. Matches with COMP0 and COMP1 set INTFLAG.CMP0 and CMP1 on the next CLK_RTC_CNT rising edge.

With CTRL.MODE = 2 the counter, fed 1 Hz, holds seconds, minutes and hours (12 or 24 hour by CTRL.CLKREP, changed only while disabled) and day of month from 1, month from 1 (January) and a year offset from a software-defined reference, read and written as one 32-bit CLOCK value. Every year divisible by 4 is taken as a leap year, so the reference must be a leap year such as 2000. After 23:59:59 on 31 December of year 63 it wraps to 00:00:00 on 1 January of year 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. A match with ALARM0, over the fields chosen by MASK0.SEL, sets INTFLAG.ALARM0 on the next CLK_RTC_CNT edge, 1 s later at 1 Hz. CTRL.MATCHCLR = 1 clears the counter on the cycle after an ALARM0 match, setting ALARM0 and OVF together.

Interrupt sources, all asynchronous and able to wake the device from any sleep mode: overflow (OVF), compare n (CMPn), alarm n (ALARMn) and synchronization ready (SYNCRDY), combined into one NVIC request. Output events, made like the interrupts and each turned on by its EVCTRL.xxxEO bit: overflow, period n (PERn, a prescaler bit toggling), compare n and alarm n. The RTC runs in any sleep mode where its clock does. On wake-up an interrupt is taken if the NVIC is set for it; otherwise the CPU resumes at the instruction after the one that entered sleep. Periodic events can wake the CPU through the event system's interrupt, with the event routed to a channel whose interrupt is enabled.

STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once when a synchronized operation starts and clears when it ends, and INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end; a synchronized access while SYNCBUSY is set stalls the bus and the CPU, with interrupts pending. Synchronized on write: CTRL.SWRST, CTRL.ENABLE, COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR and MASKn. Synchronized on read: COUNT and CLOCK.

Any of the upper eight prescaler bits (bits 2 to 9) can make a periodic event for a system tick: with EVCTRL.PEREOn = 1 an event fires on each rising edge of that bit, so PER0 fires every 8 GCLK_RTC cycles, PER1 every 16 and so on. The events do not depend on the counter's prescaler setting, except that with CTRL.PRESCALER = 0 none are made.

Digital correction trims a fast or slow oscillator in steps of about 1 ppm; it needs CTRL.PRESCALER greater than 1. Once every 4096 GCLK_RTC cycles a single prescaler count is added or skipped, FREQCORR.VALUE times over 240 such periods. FREQCORR.SIGN sets the direction: positive adds counts, lengthening the period and lowering the frequency; negative removes counts and raises it. The correction also moves the periodic events: the interval around the end of a correction cycle may be shorter or longer.

The DMAC holds a DMA engine and a CRC engine. It moves data between memories and peripherals, including between communication peripherals, without the CPU. Each channel takes transfer triggers and requests the arbiter, which makes one channel active at a time; the fetch engine loads that channel's transfer descriptor from SRAM and the channel moves the data. A higher-priority channel can interrupt an active one: the DMAC writes the active descriptor back to SRAM and starts the other. A finished transfer can raise interrupts and events. Bus interfaces: the data transfer bus, the APB bridge for its registers (an APB client), the descriptor fetch bus and the write-back bus (AHB hosts). The CRC engine lets software check transferred data for errors.

Transfers between any pair of memory and peripheral, in either direction, including memory to memory and peripheral to peripheral. Triggers from software, the event system or dedicated peripheral requests. Descriptors in SRAM: single transfers, or multi-buffer and circular buffers by linking descriptors. Up to 12 channels, each with automatic descriptor fetch and suspend/resume. Four priority levels per channel, fixed or round-robin within a level. 1 to 256 KB in one block. Static or configurable increment addressing. Optional interrupts on block complete, error and channel suspend. Four event inputs, one for each of channels 0-3, starting normal, periodic or conditional transfers or suspending and resuming the channel. Four event outputs, one for each of channels 0-3, on AHB, block or transaction transfer complete. A write-back area per channel holding the ongoing descriptor, for error handling. CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3) chosen in software.

The DMAC keeps working in IDLE 0 where its clock runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events act without waking it. Every reset returns its registers to reset values. CLK_DMAC_APB and the module clock CLK_DMAC_AHB must be enabled in the PM; the APB clock is in step with the AHB clock, may be divided and can run with the module clock off. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. Channels 0-3 can generate and use events. The DMAC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL makes it run on. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTPEND, CHID and CHINTFLAG.

A beat is one bus access, sized by BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A burst is a number of beats that cannot be interrupted. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and can be interrupted between bursts. A transaction is all the blocks of a linked list of descriptors. A descriptor must stay in SRAM. A trigger (software, event or peripheral) makes the channel request the arbiter; the granted channel runs its descriptor, can be preempted by a higher-priority channel after any burst, and resumes its block when granted again. Each beat can give an output event; each block can give interrupts and an output event. At the end of a transaction the channel is suspended or disabled, as configured. The CRC engine computes CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3) on a chosen DMA channel or on data written through its I/O interface.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR can be written only with the DMA disabled (CTRL.DMAENABLE = 0); CTRL.SWRST only with both DMA and CRC disabled; CHCTRLB (except CMD and LVL) and CHCTRLA.SWRST only with the channel disabled; CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only with the CRC disabled. Before enabling the DMAC: write the descriptor section address to BASEADDR, the write-back section address to WRBADDR, and enable each priority level wanted with CTRL.LVLENx. Before enabling a channel: write its number to CHID, choose CHCTRLB.TRIGACT and TRIGSRC, and prepare its first descriptor with BTCTRL.BEATSIZE, BTCTRL.VALID = 1, BTCNT, SRCADDR and DSTADDR. Before enabling the CRC: choose CRCCTRL.CRCSRC, CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY and, for I/O input, CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE. CTRL.DMAENABLE, CHCTRLA.ENABLE (after writing CHID.ID) and CTRL.CRCENABLE turn each on and off. CTRL.SWRST resets every DMAC register except DBGCTRL; CHCTRLA.SWRST (after CHID.ID, channel disabled) resets one channel.

A channel's first descriptor must be valid (BTCTRL.VALID) before the channel is enabled and triggered. All descriptors live in SRAM. BASEADDR points at channel 0's first descriptor; the first descriptors of all channels sit together in channel order. WRBADDR points at channel 0's ongoing descriptor in the write-back section, also in channel order. Both sections grow with the highest channel enabled, so using the lowest-numbered channels saves memory. The two sections can be separate or the same (BASEADDR = WRBADDR); separate sections let a channel repeat a transaction without rewriting its first descriptor and shorten the time from fetching the first descriptor to the first burst. Each descriptor holds BTCTRL, BTCNT, SRCADDR, DSTADDR and DESCADDR, the address of the next descriptor (0 for the last).

An enabled, unsuspended channel that gets a trigger joins the queue of pending channels and its PENDCH bit sets; the bit clears when the arbiter grants it. BUSYCH sets on its first granted burst and stays set while it goes back to the queue, and clears when it waits for a new trigger or is suspended or disabled. A channel suspended while pending leaves the queue with PENDCH still set and rejoins on resume; one disabled while pending leaves the queue and PENDCH clears. ACTIVE.LVLEXx shows a level with a channel pending or transferring. Each channel has one of four levels (CHCTRLB.LVL); with all levels enabled (CTRL.LVLENx) a higher number wins. Within a level, PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx = 0 gives static order, lowest channel number first, which can starve high numbers; RRLVLENx = 1 gives round robin, where the last channel granted, kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx, goes last next time.

When a channel is granted, its descriptor is fetched over the fetch bus into the active channel's store: from the descriptor section for a new block, from the write-back section for a block under way. Over the data bus each beat takes data at the current source address and stores it at the current destination address. Arbitration runs after every burst: if the same channel wins, BTCNT drops by the beats of a burst, the beat event fires if enabled, and the next burst runs; if another wins, BTCNT is written back before the new descriptor is fetched. When BTCNT reaches zero, BTCTRL.VALID clears and the descriptor is written back; the transfer-complete and suspend interrupts and the block event follow if enabled. After the last block DESCADDR is 0x00000000 and the channel is suspended or disabled according to BTCTRL.BLOCKACT; otherwise the next descriptor is fetched and written to the write-back section before arbitration picks the next channel.

A transfer starts only on a request, from software, a peripheral or an event (CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC), once the channel is granted. CHCTRLB.TRIGACT sets what one trigger moves: a block (0x0, the default), a beat (0x2) or a whole transaction (0x3). With one descriptor the channel disables itself after its block; with a linked list it disables after the last descriptor and otherwise waits for the next block trigger. A request that arrives during a transfer is held pending (CHSTATUS.PEND); only one is held per channel and further requests are lost. CHSTATUS.BUSY is set from start to completion of the trigger action. PENDCH and BUSYCH gather the flags of all channels.

Each block has a source (SRCADDR) and a destination (DSTADDR), each fixed or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC = 1 increments the source, by one beat when BTCTRL.STEPSEL = 0 or by 2^STEPSIZE beats when STEPSEL = 1. BTCTRL.DSTINC = 1 increments the destination, by 2^STEPSIZE beats when STEPSEL = 0 or by one beat when STEPSEL = 1; the step size applies to one side only. With incrementing on, SRCADDR and DSTADDR are set from the start address, BTCNT, the beat size and the step as given in the address equations. STEPSIZE = 0x1 gives a step of two beats on the side that uses the step size.

A bus error from an AHB client during a transfer disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR (with an interrupt if enabled); the counter is not decremented and its value is written back before the channel stops. Fetching a descriptor with BTCTRL.VALID = 0, or resuming into a next-descriptor address of 0x00000000, suspends the channel and sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR, with the suspend interrupt if enabled.

A transaction of several blocks uses linked descriptors: after each block the DMAC fetches the descriptor at DESCADDR, until a block whose DESCADDR is 0x00000000 ends the transaction. To append, build the new descriptor with DESCADDR = 0 and point the current last descriptor at it. To change a list in use: enable the channel's suspend interrupt and the channel; build the new descriptor (DESCADDR, DSTADDR, SRCADDR, BTCTRL with optional suspend block action, VALID set); clear VALID on the list and on the descriptor to update; read DESCADDR from write-back memory. If the DMAC has not yet fetched the descriptor to change, update its DESCADDR in the list, optionally clear the suspend action, set VALID and optionally resume. If it is running that descriptor, issue a suspend command and wait for the interrupt, update DESCADDR in write-back memory, clear the interrupt and resume, then update the list copy, optionally clear the suspend action and set VALID. To insert C between A and B: impossible while B runs; if A has not started, clear A's VALID, point A at C and C at B, set A's VALID; if A is running, suspend the channel, do the same, then resume.

Writing the suspend command to CHCTRLB.CMD suspends the channel after the burst under way, clears the command, sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and raises the suspend interrupt if enabled. BTCTRL.BLOCKACT = 0x2 or 0x3 suspends the channel after a block: it stays enabled and still takes triggers but leaves arbitration. Fetching an invalid descriptor also suspends it and sets CHSTATUS.FERR. Only enabled channels can be suspended; a suspend aimed at a disabled channel is ignored. The resume command in CHCTRLB.CMD restarts a suspended channel where it stopped; given before a suspend, it makes the channel skip the next suspend and carry on.

Normal transfer: the event triggers a beat or burst and is acknowledged at once, setting CHSTATUS.PEND and PENDCHn; an event arriving while the channel is pending is lost. Conditional transfer on strobe: for peripheral triggers such as timed protocols or periodic peripheral-to-peripheral transfers, a peripheral request is registered only when it coincides with an event after the previous action has finished; with both present PEND and PENDCHn set. Conditional transfer: each peripheral request is stored when the event comes, setting PEND and PENDCHn and acknowledging the event, as when one peripheral supplies the event and a second supplies the trigger for a transfer between them. Conditional block transfer: an event must arrive before a block starts and is acknowledged when the block ends. Channel suspend: acknowledged when the current AHB access ends. Channel resume: acknowledged at once, clearing CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip next block suspend: resumes a channel already suspended, or else is held until the next block suspend, which is then skipped. In the three conditional modes a software trigger also starts a transfer.

Event outputs exist only on the lowest-numbered channels and are one AHB clock wide. CHCTRLB.EVOE = 1 enables them and BTCTRL.EVOSEL picks after each block (0x1) or each beat (0x3); for an event at the end of a transaction, select the block event in the last descriptor only. Disabling a channel aborts its transfers cleanly, and disabling the DMAC aborts all: the active channel stops after its current beat once the write-back section is updated, the other channels stop on the next clock, and CHCTRLA.ENABLE (or CTRL.DMAENABLE) clears when done.

The CRC engine computes CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT, polynomial with terms of degree 16, 12, 5 and 0, 0x1021) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3, polynomial with terms of degree 32, 26, 23, 22, 16, 12, 11, 10, 8, 7, 5, 4, 2, 1 and 0, 0x04C11DB7); CRC-n detects every error burst of n bits or less and a fraction 1 - 2^-n of longer ones. CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY chooses (CRC-16 by default) and CRCCTRL.CRCSRC takes data from one DMA channel or from the APB interface. The result is in CRCCHKSUM; a CRC-32 result reads bit-reversed and complemented. The engine works a byte at a time. On a DMA channel it uses the channel's beat size and runs on everything passing through, ready when the transaction completes or is aborted; SRAM, Flash or I/O data can be checked by sending them through a channel to CRCDATAIN. From the CPU, set CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE (8, 16 or 32 bits) and write data to CRCDATAIN: a 32-bit write takes four cycles, CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY signals the calculation and new data may be written only when it is clear.

Per-channel interrupt sources: transfer complete (TCMPL, a block finished), transfer error (TERR, a bus error in a burst or an invalid descriptor) and channel suspend (SUSP), in CHINTFLAG with CHINTENSET and CHINTENCLR, combined into one NVIC request. INTSTATUS shows which channels have interrupts pending and CHINTFLAG which condition; INTPEND gives the lowest channel with one pending and its flags. Output event CH on block or beat completion, enabled by CHCTRLB.EVOE and chosen by BTCTRL.EVOSEL. Input event actions, enabled by EVIE: TRIG, CTRIG, CBLOCK, SUSPEND, RESUME, SSKIP and INCPRI (raise channel priority); several can be enabled and any enabled action is taken for any incoming event. Events exist only on some channels. The DMAC runs in IDLE 0, does not transfer in IDLE 1 and IDLE 2 because the AHB clocks stop, and in standby is disabled internally while keeping its settings.

The external interrupt controller turns up to 16 pins (EXTINTx) into interrupt lines, plus a non-maskable pin (NMI) wired to the CPU's NMI request so it can interrupt anything. Each line is masked on its own and fires on a rising edge, a falling edge, both edges, a high level or a low level, with an optional spike filter; lines can work asynchronously so they wake the device from sleep with every clock stopped, and each EXTINT can make an event.

The pins must be set up in PORT. Every interrupt works down to STANDBY, and the EIC can mask some automatically so they do not wake the device; it runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its events act without waking. CLK_EIC_APB is masked in the PM; GCLK_EIC, asynchronous to the bus, must be set up in GCLK when needed. EXTINT and NMI have their own request lines to the NVIC; NMI needs no NVIC set-up. Events need the event system set up first. The EIC keeps running with the CPU halted by a debugger. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG and NMIFLAG.

Order: enable CLK_EIC_APB; enable GCLK_EIC if edge detection or filtering is used; write EVCTRL, WAKEUP and CONFIGy; enable the EIC (CTRL.ENABLE). For NMI, enable GCLK_EIC after writing NMICTRL. CTRL.SWRST resets and disables it. CONFIGn.SENSEx chooses each pin's sense, and INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] sets when it is met. After the flag is cleared, an edge-sensitive line waits for a new edge, while a level-sensitive line sets again at once if the level is still there. CONFIGn.FILTENx = 1 adds a majority filter that samples the pin three times on GCLK_EIC and passes the value that at least two samples share. Level detection without filter is asynchronous and needs no GCLK_EIC; with edge detection or filtering the EIC requests GCLK_EIC itself, which must be enabled in GCLK.

The NMI pin also senses edges or levels, set in NMICTRL.NMISENSE, with a filter enabled by NMICTRL.NMIFILTEN; edge detection or filtering needs GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K. NMISENSE alone turns detection on; the EIC need not be enabled. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always requests an interrupt.
