Interrupt sources are the EXTINTx pins (flags in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR) and NMI (NMIFLAG, always enabled), with one request line per EXTINT and one for NMI. When one EXTINT is offered on two or more pins, only the first programmed is active. EVCTRL.EXTINTEO enables an event from a pin whenever its CONFIGn condition is met. In sleep a pin wakes the device when its condition is met, its INTENSET bit is set and WAKEUP.WAKEUPEN[x] = 1; WAKEUPEN without the interrupt enable is not advised. CTRL.SWRST and CTRL.ENABLE are write-synchronized through STATUS.SYNCBUSY; an access needing synchronization while it is set stalls the bus and CPU.

The NVM is Flash that keeps code and data with power off: a main array and a smaller EEPROM emulation array (RWWEE, read-while-write)  that can be programmed while the main array is read. The controller reads and writes over a 32-bit AHB interface and takes commands and settings over a 32-bit APB interface. Every NVM section, calibration and configuration included, is mapped on the AHB. It has programmable read wait states, 16 regions each lockable, extra protection for a bootloader, device protection by a security bit, power-down of Flash in sleep through the PM with wake-up on sleep exit or on first access, and a direct-mapped cache. A register marked enable-protected can hold bits that are not.

The controller runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupt can wake the device. On entering sleep the PM puts the NVM in low power according to CTRLB.SLEEPPRM, and always in STANDBY. Page buffer contents are lost in low power, so a write command must be given first; disabling SLEEPPRM keeps it through sleep, but nothing keeps it through STANDBY. It uses CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB; when the AHB frequency changes, the read wait states must suit it (the electrical characteristics give the number per frequency range). The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. It runs normally in debug mode; with the security bit set the NVM cannot be accessed. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG and STATUS. After power-up it runs a power-up sequence, holding AHB accesses, then works without configuration.

The NVM is made of rows of four pages: a row is the erase unit and a page the write unit, so one erase clears four pages and four writes fill the row. The calibration and auxiliary space (factory calibration and system configuration, at NVM base + 0x00800000) and the RWWEE space (at NVM base + 0x00400000) are memory mapped above the main space and read over AHB like it. The lowest rows of the main space can be made a bootloader section with the BOOTPROT fuses, protected by its region lock bits and BOOTPROT[2:0]; the top rows can be made an EEPROM emulation section, writable whatever the region locks.

The NVM is split into 16 equal regions, each with a lock bit that blocks writing and erasing its pages; all are unlocked from the factory. The Lock Region and Unlock Region commands act on the region holding the address in ADDR (written by software or left by the last write) until the next reset or the next command; LOCK shows the state. The default lock state is changed by writing the user configuration in the auxiliary space with the Write Auxiliary Page command, which takes effect after the next reset.

Reads and automatic page writes go straight to the main or RWWEE address space over AHB; manual page writes, row erases and the rest are commands written to CTRLA.CMD together with the CTRLA.CMDEX key. INTFLAG.READY is low until a command finishes, and commands written meanwhile are ignored. CTRLB sets the power reduction mode, read wait states and write mode. Read data arrive after CTRLB.RWS wait states. Reading the main array during a program or erase of the main array stalls the bus until it ends; it does not stall during programming or erasing of the RWWEE array. RWWEE reads time like main reads for byte and half-word accesses, with a data phase twice as long for word accesses; the RWWEE cannot be read during a main-array write or erase, though RWWEE programming and erasing may run during main-array reads. The RWWEE space is not cached, so frequent access costs speed and current.

Flash must be erased before programming: a debugger chip erase clears the main and RWWEE spaces, or Erase Row and RWWEE Erase Row clear single rows. After programming, the region holding a page can be locked against stray writes. Data go first to a page-sized buffer, shared by the main and RWWEE arrays, by 16- or 32-bit writes; an 8-bit write causes a system exception. Each AHB write stores its address in ADDR; once loaded, that page goes to Flash with the Write Page or RWWEE Write Page command and the CMDEX key. STATUS.LOAD shows a loaded buffer. With CTRLB.MANW = 0 a page is written automatically when its last location is written; a partly filled page needs a manual write. Manual write (MANW = 1): erase the row, fill the buffer through the main address space, issue Write Page with CMDEX, then do one read on the NVMCTRL AHB0 interface as a read memory barrier; READY stays low and AHB access stalls during programming. Automatic write: erase the row before the last buffer write, then fill the buffer; the write starts on the last location, with READY low and AHB stalled meanwhile.

operation.topic: NVM page buffer, erase and power reduction
operation.text: After a page write the buffer holds all ones; Page Buffer Clear empties a partly written buffer. Erase Row (or RWWEE Erase Row) sets every bit of the row addressed by ADDR (any address in the row; ADDR.ADDR counts 16-bit words) to 1; in a locked region nothing is erased and STATUS.LOCKE sets. Two commands (set and clear power reduction mode) move the controller and Flash in and out of power reduction, shown by STATUS.PRM. The user configuration lives in the auxiliary space; the bootloader starts at offset 0 of the main array and its section is write-protected.

The security bit locks the whole chip against external access. The Set Security Bit (SSB) command sets it; only a debugger chip erase clears it; STATUS.PROGE can be checked after SSB. Enabling BOD33 while the security bit is set raises the protection. The cache lowers current and raises speed when wait states are needed; it covers only the main array, is direct-mapped with 8 lines of 64 bits (64 bytes), is enabled by CTRLB.CACHEDIS = 0 and has three modes set by CTRLB.READMODE. The INVALL command invalidates every line; commands that change NVM contents invalidate lines automatically.

PORT drives the I/O pins, organised in groups of up to 32 pins each (the number of groups follows the package). Each pin is general-purpose I/O under software control or is handed to a peripheral; as I/O it is an input or output with configurable drive and pull. Set, clear and toggle registers for direction and output value (DIRSET/DIRCLR/DIRTGL, OUTSET/OUTCLR/OUTTGL) change chosen pins in one atomic 8-, 16- or 32-bit write without touching the others. PORT sits on the bus matrix behind an AHB/APB bridge, and DIR, OUT and IN can also be reached over the CPU's single-cycle local bus (IOBUS). Other features: peripheral multiplexing in software, a configuration register per pin, push-pull output, pull-up or pull-down, drive strength, input sampling control, and an input buffer that can be turned off to save current.

Lines are named by group letter and two-digit number (A24, C03) and pins Pxy (PA24, PC03); some lines are not present on every device. A pin can be routed through one or more peripheral multiplexer settings, and the selected peripheral then controls the pad's output and can read it. During reset every line is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull all off. PORT runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs. CLK_PORT_APB (which may be divided from the CPU clock) gives register access through the bus matrix; an AHB clock, the PORT's internal clock, serves IOBUS accesses. IOBUS accesses take priority, so an APB access can see one cycle of latency when both happen. PORT has no DMA, interrupts or events, keeps running in debug, and every writable register can be PAC-protected. Selecting an analog function on a pin turns off its digital features; analog signals reach the pads on analog buses.

The IOBUS links the CPU straight to PORT as a single-cycle bus with no wait states, for 8-, 16- and 32-bit accesses: DIR and OUT can be read, written, set, cleared and toggled and IN read. As it cannot wait for IN to resynchronize, pins read through IOBUS must be set to continuous sampling in CTRL, or stale values are read.

Each group of up to 32 pins has its own copy of the PORT registers, the group x set at PORT + 0x80 × group index (A is 0, B is 1). DIR bit y = 1 makes pin y an output, driven to the OUT bit; DIR = 0 makes it an input. IN gives the pin value, resynchronized to the PORT clock, whether input or output, but only if PINCFGy.INEN = 1. By default the input synchronizer runs only when IN is read, delaying the read by two PORT clock cycles; CTRL.SAMPLINGn keeps the synchronizers of a group of eight pins always running, at the cost of current. PINCFGy (at byte offset PINCFG0 + y) holds PMUXEN, which hands the pin to the peripheral chosen in PMUXn (PMUXE or PMUXO at byte offset PMUX0 + y/2); the peripheral must be set up and enabled too. After reset all ordinary pads belong to PORT, outputs in high impedance and input buffers off, even with no clock running; pins with special roles, such as the debugger pins, can start differently.

PINCFGy sets push-pull or pull configuration, so no intermediate states appear while direction and value change. With pull enabled the OUT bit chooses pull-up (1) or pull-down (0). A push-pull output drives low or high from OUT, limited only by the pin's own capability; enabling the output driver turns pull off. An input with no pull and nothing external floats. With input, output and pull all off the pin has no digital function (the reset and analog state). Access priority: the CPU over IOBUS first (it cannot wait), then APB.

The event system passes signals (events) between peripherals with low latency and without the CPU, the buses or RAM. Event generators make events under conditions particular to each peripheral; event users act on them; a peripheral can be both. It has 12 channels, each able to take any generator over an asynchronous, resynchronized or synchronous path, 74 generators and 29 users, an edge detector, software events, and SleepWalking and interrupts for use in sleep. Each user picks one channel and several users can share a channel. A generator can feed several channels, but a channel takes one generator.

EVSYS can wake the CPU from any sleep mode even with its channel clocks and bus clock off; in sleep the device can restart the EVSYS clock, and some generators make events with their own clocks stopped. CLK_EVSYS_APB is masked in the PM. Each channel has its own generic clock, GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n, for detection and propagation, set up in GCLK before use. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC. EVSYS keeps running with the CPU halted in debug, and can be made to halt. Write access can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG.

Configure the user multiplexer before the channel. USER takes the channel (USER.CHANNEL) and the user (USER.USER) in one 16-bit write; to read a user's setting, write USER.USER with an 8-bit write and read the 16-bit register. CHANNEL takes the channel number, PATH, EDGSEL and EVGEN in one 32-bit write; to read, write CHANNEL.CHANNEL with an 8-bit write, then read. Each user has its own multiplexer that sees every channel. EVSYS is always enabled; CTRL.SWRST resets every register and cancels events in flight. Channels start unconnected (EVGEN = 0).

Asynchronous path: the event goes from generator to user untouched, with no channel clock needed and no clock latency; the channel gives no interrupts, CHSTATUS reads zero and edge detection, if any, is the user's job. With generator and user on the same generic clock it has the least latency. Synchronous path: for a generator on the same generic clock generator as the channel, and a user that supports it (otherwise use asynchronous); on different clocks a change may be missed and the event lost. Resynchronized path: for a generator on a different generic clock generator; the channel resynchronizes the event. Both clocked paths can raise interrupts and update CHSTATUS, and need edge detection: rising, falling or both (CHANNEL.EDGSEL); a pulse generator cannot use both edges and takes the edge that suits its idle level. With CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0 a clocked channel requests its generic clock only while an event passes (SleepWalking); with GCLKREQ = 1 the clock stays on.

operation.topic: EVSYS status, software events and interrupts
operation.text: For clocked paths, CHSTATUS.CHBUSYn is set while some user on channel n has yet to take its event, and CHSTATUS.USRRDYn when every user on it is ready. Writing CHANNEL.SWEVT = 1 together with CHANNEL.CHANNEL makes a software event, handled like any generator's, which needs a synchronous or resynchronized path (PATH = 0x0 or 0x1), rising-edge detection (EDGSEL = 0x1) and CTRL.GCLKREQ = 1. Interrupt sources, both asynchronous wake-up sources combined into one NVIC request: overrun channel n (OVRn), set when a user on the channel is not ready for a new event or a new event comes before every user has taken the last; and event detected channel n (EVDn), set when the channel's generator event is seen. Both flags work only on the resynchronized path and read zero on the asynchronous path.

EVSYS can wake the device from any sleep mode. When a generator makes an event with the system clock stopped, a clocked channel restarts its GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNELx without waking the system, keeps it only while the event is handled, then stops it with the device still asleep (SleepWalking); the asynchronous path needs no clock. A software reset returns every register to reset values and cancels events in flight. Registers are 8, 16 or 32 bits with atomic access of each size and direct access to their byte and half-word parts; enable-protected registers are written only with the module disabled.

Up to six SERCOM instances. Each one is set by CTRLA.MODE to be an I2C (SMBus compatible), SPI or USART interface, and once enabled all of the instance serves that one mode. Each has a transmitter with a single buffer, a receiver with a double buffer (one level in I2C, two in USART and SPI), a baud-rate generator and address match and mask logic. The serial engine runs from the internal generic clock or from an external clock; on an external clock it works in every sleep mode. DMA can serve it.

Each SERCOM has four pads, PAD[3:0]; the signals of the chosen mode are routed onto them through a multiplexer set in the mode's control registers, and the pins are given to the SERCOM in PORT. The bus clock CLK_SERCOMx_APB is masked in the PM. Two generic clocks serve it: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE, needed to run as a host, and GCLK_SERCOMx_SLOW, needed only by some functions; both are set up in GCLK first and are asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register accesses are synchronized. DMA requests go to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC; there are no events. It keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL says to halt. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR; PAC protection does not apply to debugger accesses.

The baud-rate generator runs on GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock and gives /1, /2 and /16 outputs: asynchronous transmission uses /16 and reception /1, synchronous operation uses /2, chosen automatically by the mode. Asynchronous operation has an arithmetic mode with a 16-bit BAUD value (0 to 65535); synchronous operation uses an 8-bit value (0 to 255). CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and leaves the peripheral disabled; CTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off.

Address matching (SPI and I2C) compares 7 or 8 bits according to mode, in one of three ways. Address with mask: ADDR.ADDR is compared with the received address on every bit not set in ADDR.ADDRMASK; a mask of all zeros matches one address, all ones matches every address. Two unique addresses: a match on either ADDR.ADDR or ADDR.ADDRMASK. Address range: any address from ADDR.ADDRMASK (lower limit) up to ADDR.ADDR (upper limit), both included.

Interrupt sources depend on the mode; each has a flag in INTFLAG, is enabled by INTENSET and disabled by INTENCLR, and a request lasts until its flag is cleared, it is disabled, or the SERCOM resets. INTFLAG tells which condition happened; interrupts must also be enabled globally. The SERCOM runs in any sleep mode in which its serial clock (external, or from the internal baud-rate generator) runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. Registers marked write-synchronized or read-synchronized cross the clock boundary when written or read.

The USART is a SERCOM mode: full duplex, asynchronous with clock recovery or synchronous, on an internal or external clock. Frames carry 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 data bits, LSB or MSB first, with optional odd or even parity and 1 or 2 stop bits. It detects buffer overflow and frame errors, filters noise (false start-bit detection and a digital low-pass filter), detects collisions and runs in every sleep mode. Speed reaches half the system clock with the internal clock and the system clock with an external clock. Flow control uses RTS and CTS; IrDA encoding and decoding runs up to 115.2 kbps; LIN client operation comes with auto-baud and break detection; there is also start-of-frame detection, and DMA. The transmitter has one write buffer, so frames follow with no gap; the receiver has a two-level buffer.

In USART mode the SERCOM sets each pin's direction and value. PORT PINCFGn.DRVSTR still applies to its outputs; PINCFGn.PULLEN still applies to its inputs but only switches a pull-down (no pull-up). With the receiver or transmitter disabled, its pin is free for other uses. CTRLA.TXPO and CTRLA.RXPO, with PORT, place TxD, RxD and XCK on the pads.

CLK_SERCOMx_APB is masked in the PM; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up and enabled in GCLK before use, and being asynchronous to the bus clock it makes some register writes synchronized. DMA requests need the DMAC set up, interrupts the NVIC; no events. It runs on while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL halts it. INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA cannot be PAC write-protected; other writable registers can.

A frame is one start bit (low), 5 to 9 data bits, an optional parity bit after the data and before the first stop bit, and 1 or 2 stop bits (high). The next frame may follow at once or the line may return to idle, which is high.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN and TXEN) and BAUD are enable-protected: writes while the USART is enabled or being enabled are discarded, and writes while it is being disabled take effect once disabling ends. Before enabling: set CTRLA.MODE to external (0x0) or internal (0x1) clock; CTRLA.CMODE to asynchronous (0) or synchronous (1); CTRLA.RXPO for the receive pad; CTRLA.TXPO for the transmit and clock pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE for character size; CTRLA.DORD for bit order; for parity, CTRLA.FORM = 0x1 and CTRLB.PMODE even or odd; CTRLB.SBMODE for stop bits; BAUD when the clock is internal; then CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables the USART.

In both modes the shift and sample clock comes from the baud-rate generator (CTRLA.MODE = 0x1) or from the XCK pin (CTRLA.MODE = 0x0). CTRLA.CMODE = 1 selects synchronous mode, 0 asynchronous. Asynchronous mode uses the 16-bit BAUD value; synchronous mode uses its eight low bits.

In synchronous mode CTRLA.MODE makes XCK an input or an output. RxD is sampled on the XCK edge opposite to the one on which TxD changes: with CTRLA.CPOL = 0 data changes on the rising edge and is sampled on the falling edge; with CPOL = 1 it changes on the falling edge and is sampled on the rising edge. With an external XCK (MODE = 0x0) the shift registers run straight from XCK, unsynchronized to the system clock, at up to the system frequency.

TxDATA and RxDATA share the DATA address: a write goes to TxDATA, a read returns RxDATA. A written character moves to the shift register when it is empty and is sent. INTFLAG.DRE says DATA is empty and may be written (write it only then); INTFLAG.TXC sets when a whole frame including stop bits has gone and nothing new waits. Clearing CTRLB.TXEN disables the transmitter only after the shift register and TxDATA are empty. The receiver starts on a valid start bit, samples each bit at the baud rate or on XCK and ignores a second stop bit; when the first stop bit arrives the frame moves to the two-level buffer and INTFLAG.RXC sets, after which DATA may be read. Clearing CTRLB.RXEN disables the receiver, flushes the buffer and loses any frame in progress.

STATUS holds three error bits, FERR (frame), BUFOVF (buffer overflow) and PERR (parity); each stays set until written with 1 and clears when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON = 1 BUFOVF sets at the moment of overflow and software empties the buffer by reading RxDATA until RXC clears; with IBON = 0 the overflow travels with the data through the buffer and BUFOVF and INTFLAG.ERROR set together with RXC when that data is read. Asynchronous reception uses a clock recovery unit, which locks incoming frames to the internal baud clock, and a data recovery unit, which samples and low-pass filters each bit.

Reception works only while the incoming rate stays close enough to the internal baud rate for the receiver to lock to the start bit; the mismatch comes from reference clock instability and from the baud-rate generator not dividing exactly, so BAUD is set for the least error. The recommended receiver errors assume receiver and transmitter share the total error equally and include clock-source and baud-generator error. Worked example at 3 Mbps (48 MHz, BAUD = 0, 16 samples, 10 data bits, no parity, one start and one stop bit): the receiver accepts +3.3 %/−4.35 %; with a DFLL source at ±0.3 % the receiver error is +3.0 %/−4.05 %, and the recommended maximum Rx error is ±1.5 %. The transmitter's error should lie within the recommended Rx error; larger errors work if they stay inside the accepted receiver error.

CTRLA.FORM = 0x1 adds a parity bit. Even parity (CTRLB.PMODE = 0) makes the count of ones including the parity bit even; odd parity (PMODE = 1) makes it odd. On reception the parity is recomputed and a mismatch sets STATUS.PERR.

RTS and CTS cross over to the remote device (TXD to RXD, RXD to TXD, CTS to RTS, RTS to CTS). It works only with the internal clock (CTRLA.MODE = 1), asynchronous mode (CMODE = 0) and the flow-control pinout (CTRLA.TXPO = 2). The receiver drives RTS high while it is disabled or its buffer is full; changing CTRLB.RXEN moves RTS after a synchronization delay, a full buffer raises RTS at once and the frame then arriving waits in the shift register until there is room. STATUS.CTS shows the CTS input; a character starts only while CTS = 0, and when CTS rises the frame in progress finishes and transmission stops.

IrDA encoding up to 115.2 kb/s needs CTRLB.ENC = 1, asynchronous mode and 16x sampling (CTRLA.SAMPR[0] = 0). Each zero bit is sent as a high pulse 3/16 of a bit period wide. The decoder resynchronizes its baud counter at the start of every zero pulse and accepts a pulse at least as long as RXPL.RXPL sets, passing it on at half a bit time; transmit and receive polarities are opposite (a sent 0 is a 1 pulse, an accepted 0 pulse is received as 0). Example: RXPL = 19 requires pulses of at least 20 serial-engine clocks, which with BAUD = 0xE666 (160 clocks per bit) is 2/16 of a bit.

Available with the auto-baud frame format (CTRLA.FORM = 0x04 or 0x05), asynchronous mode and 16x fractional sampling (CTRLA.SAMPR = 1). More than 11 consecutive dominant bits at the set baud rate are a break field: INTFLAG.RXBRK sets and a sync character of 0x55 is expected. A counter runs over the 8 bit times of the sync field; its 13 upper bits (count / 8) become BAUD.BAUD and its 3 lower bits BAUD.FP, loaded after a synchronization delay. A sync character other than 0x55 sets STATUS.ISF and INTFLAG.ERROR and leaves the baud rate as it was. Data characters follow the break and sync fields.

With receiver and transmitter both enabled and joined (by pinout or outside), CTRLB.COLDEN = 1 compares each sent bit with the received one; reception while the transmitter is idle is no collision. On a collision the USART aborts the transfer, flushes the transmit buffer, clears CTRLB.TXEN after a synchronization delay (SYNCBUSY.CTRLB set meanwhile; TxD then tri-stated), sets STATUS.COLL and INTFLAG.ERROR, and sets INTFLAG.TXC. Software re-enables the transmitter once SYNCBUSY.CTRLB is clear.

operation.topic: USART loop-back, start-of-frame detection and sample adjustment
operation.text: Loop-back: CTRLA.RXPO and TXPO on the same pad; the loop runs through the pad, so the signal also appears outside. Start-of-frame detection (CTRLB.SFDE = 1), in asynchronous and synchronous modes, wakes on a start bit: a falling edge on RxD powers up the 8 MHz internal oscillator and the USART clock, and the frame is received if the baud rate is slow enough for the oscillator's start-up time, which varies with supply and temperature; in standby the fast-start internal oscillator must be the GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE source. With INTENSET.RXS set the Receive Start interrupt fires at once; without it the oscillator and clock stay on through the frame and the CPU wakes on Receive Complete. Sample adjustment: asynchronous reception votes over three middle samples chosen by CTRLA.SAMPA; with SAMPA = 0 these are samples 7-8-9 at 16x and 3-4-5 at 8x. Since a frame start need not align with the reference clock edge, the first count can last less than one reference period.

DMA RX request: set while the receive buffer holds data, cleared by reading DATA. DMA TX request: set while TX DATA is empty, cleared by writing DATA. Interrupts DRE, RXC, TXC, RXS, CTSIC, RXBRK and ERROR are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode; each has an INTFLAG flag, INTENSET and INTENCLR bits, and stays requested until cleared, disabled or reset. No events.

Internal clock with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE can run in every sleep mode and any interrupt wakes the device. External clock with RUNSTDBY = 1: Receive Start and Receive Complete can wake it. Internal clock with RUNSTDBY = 0: the clock stops after the transfer in progress, and Receive Start and Receive Complete can wake it. External clock with RUNSTDBY = 0: the external clock is disconnected after the transfer in progress and all reception is dropped. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN are synchronized (RXEN in a slightly different way).

SPI is a SERCOM mode: full duplex on four wires (MISO, MOSI, SCK, SS), with one transmit buffer and a receive buffer two deep, all four SPI modes, LSB or MSB first, 8- or 9-bit characters and DMA. Running in one data direction frees the MISO or MOSI pin for another function. As host it has an 8-bit clock generator and hardware-controlled SS, with fSCK = 1/tSCK; as client it takes fSCK = 1/tSSCK, offers optional 8-bit address match, runs in every sleep mode and wakes on an SS transition. tSCK and tSSCK are given in the SPI timing characteristics.

In SPI mode the SERCOM sets each pin's direction and value; PORT DRVSTR still applies to outputs, and PULLEN on inputs only switches a pull-down. With the receiver disabled the data input pin is free. As host, SS is driven by hardware when CTRLB.MSSEN = 1. CTRLA.DIPO and CTRLA.DOPO, with PORT, place the signals on the pads. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE clocks the SPI and must be enabled in GCLK; CLK_SERCOMx_APB is masked in the PM. DMA needs the DMAC, interrupts the NVIC; no events. It runs while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL halts it. INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA cannot be PAC write-protected.

As host the SPI starts and clocks every transaction. A transaction is one or more characters of 8 or 9 bits framed by SS low. With several clients the host pulls the chosen client's SS low; with a single client SS may be tied low. Data goes host to client on MOSI and client to host on MISO, one character each way at a time; the host raises SS to end the transaction. DATA can take the next character while the current one shifts.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN), BAUD and ADDR are enable-protected: writes while enabled or being enabled are discarded; writes while being disabled complete afterwards. Set CTRLA.MODE to 0x2 (client) or 0x3 (host); CPOL and CPHA; CTRLA.FORM; CTRLA.DIPO for the receive pad and CTRLA.DOPO for the transmit pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE; CTRLA.DORD; as host, BAUD and, for hardware SS, CTRLB.MSSEN = 1; then CTRLB.RXEN = 1. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL.

As host (CTRLA.MODE = 0x3) SCK comes from the baud-rate generator in synchronous mode, using the 8-bit BAUD value. As client (MODE = 0x2) the host's SCK clocks the shift register. TxDATA and RxDATA share the DATA address.

With CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 the hardware drives SS; with MSSEN = 0, SS is any general-purpose output that software pulls low before and high after the transaction. A character written to DATA moves to the shift register, then INTFLAG.DRE sets and the next may be written. As each character shifts out one shifts in; with the receiver enabled it moves to the receive buffer in the clock cycle of its last bit and INTFLAG.RXC sets. INTFLAG.TXC sets when the last character has gone and DATA holds nothing.

While SS is high the client stays inactive with MISO tri-stated, and DATA may be written whenever INTFLAG.DRE is set. With SS low and SCK running it samples and shifts in the selected mode; DRE sets when TxDATA loads into the shift register; each received character enters the receive buffer in the clock cycle of its last bit and RXC sets; TXC sets when the host raises SS. A DATA write takes up to three SCK cycles to be ready for the next character boundary, so the first character of a transaction is not DATA unless the shift register was preloaded; within a transaction each next character must be written with at least three SCK cycles of the current one left, or the previous received character is sent. DRE sets three CLK_SERCOM_APB cycles after DATA empties.

The only error bit is STATUS.BUFOVF, kept until written with 1 and cleared when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON = 1 it sets at once on overflow and software reads RxDATA until RXC clears; with IBON = 0 the overflow travels with the data and BUFOVF and INTFLAG.ERROR set with RXC when it is read, and RxDATA is zero.

As client (MODE = 0x2) with CTRLA.FORM = 0x2, the first character of each transaction is checked against the address logic. On a match RXC sets, MISO is enabled and the transaction proceeds, and a match can wake the device from sleep; with no match the whole transaction is ignored. With 9-bit characters only the lower 8 bits are compared with ADDR. Preload must be off (CTRLB.PLOADEN = 0).

A client first sends what is in its shift register: the reset value, or the last character of the previous transaction. With CTRLB.PLOADEN = 1 one character written while the synchronized SS is high is loaded into the shift register, so no dummy character starts the transaction; a second character written before SS falls waits in DATA. Enough time must pass between SS falling and the first SCK sampling edge for SS to synchronize to the system clock plus the MISO-to-SCK setup time; the electrical characteristics give the timing.

Clients in parallel need CTRLB.MSSEN = 0: the host drives a separate SS to each from general-purpose pins, and the one selected drives the shared tri-state MISO. Clients in series (daisy chain) share one SS, hardware or software controlled, and the host shifts n characters for n clients. Loop-back: DIPO and DOPO on the same pad; the loop runs through the pad and is visible outside.

operation.topic: SPI hardware SS and select-low detection
operation.text: With CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 the host drives SS low at least one baud cycle before the transfer and keeps it low at least one baud cycle after; between back-to-back frames SS goes high for at least one baud cycle. Each of these gaps, T, is one to two baud cycles depending on the transfer mode. As client, CTRLB.SSDE = 1 makes a falling SS set INTFLAG.SSL and wake the device.

operation.topic: SPI DMA, interrupts, sleep and synchronization
operation.text: DMA RX is set while the receive buffer holds data and cleared by reading DATA; DMA TX is set while TX DATA is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupts DRE, RXC, TXC, SSL and ERROR are asynchronous and wake the device from any sleep mode; enabled ones read back from INTENSET or INTENCLR. Host with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE runs in idle and standby and any interrupt wakes the device. Host with RUNSTDBY = 0: the clock stops after the transaction in progress; any interrupt wakes it. Client with RUNSTDBY = 1: Receive Complete wakes it. Client with RUNSTDBY = 0: all reception, the transaction in progress included, is dropped. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE and CTRLB.RXEN are synchronized (RXEN in a slightly different way).

I2C is a SERCOM mode, host or client, compatible with Philips I2C, SMBus and PMBus, at 100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz and 3.4 MHz, with 4-wire operation, slew-rate limited outputs, filtered inputs and DMA. The host uses the baud-rate generator; the client uses the address match logic, works in every sleep mode, wakes on address match and matches 7- and 10-bit addresses in hardware: a unique address and/or the 7-bit general call address, an address range, or two unique addresses.

In I2C mode the SERCOM sets the pins' direction and value; with receiver or transmitter disabled the pins are free. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE clocks the host; GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW is needed only for some functions such as SMBus timing; both are set up in GCLK before use and are asynchronous to CLK_SERCOMx_APB, which is masked in the PM. DMA needs the DMAC, interrupts the NVIC; no events. It runs on while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL halts it. INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR cannot be PAC write-protected.

SDA carries data and SCL the clock. The host sends a start condition, a 7-bit address and a direction bit; the addressed client acknowledges and data packets follow, each 8 data bits and an ACK or NACK bit. After a NACK from either side the host ends with a stop condition or sends a repeated start to transfer more.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except ACKACT and CMD), BAUD, and ADDR in client operation are enable-protected. Set CTRLA.MODE to 0x4 (client) or 0x5 (host); optionally CTRLA.SDAHOLD, CTRLB.SMEN (smart mode) and CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN (SCL low time-out). As host, set CTRLA.INACTOUT (inactive bus time-out) and BAUD; as client, CTRLB.AMODE and ADDR.ADDR and ADDR.ADDRMASK. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL.

Start and stop detectors and a bit counter track the bus in every sleep mode while the GCLK_SERCOM clocks run; STATUS.BUSSTATE reads the state, and the state machine runs while the host is enabled. After enable it is UNKNOWN (0b00); it goes to IDLE (0b01) when 0b01 is written to BUSSTATE, a stop condition is seen, or the inactive bus time-out set for SMBus (CTRLA.INACTOUT) expires, and never returns to UNKNOWN. A start from another host makes it BUSY (0b11) until a stop or a time-out. Writing ADDR.ADDR while IDLE sends a start and enters OWNER (0b10); a stop at the end returns to IDLE. A collision while OWNER means arbitration is lost and the state is BUSY until a stop; a repeated start changes the state only if arbitration is lost during it. A protocol violation can hang the I2C; CTRLA.SWRST recovers it.

The host is byte oriented and interrupt driven, with most events handled automatically and a smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN) that triggers operations on its own. With CTRLA.SCLSM = 0 the clock is held low either ahead of or behind the ACK bit; with SCLSM = 1 interrupts come only after the ACK bit, for use when DATA need not be checked before acknowledging. High-speed mode needs SCLSM = 1.

operation.topic: I2C host clock, Sm, Fm and Fm+
operation.text: Modes: standard (Sm) up to 100 kHz, fast (Fm) up to 400 kHz, fast plus (Fm+) up to 1 MHz, high speed (Hs) up to 3.4 MHz. In Sm, Fm and Fm+, BAUD sets the SCL low and high times and the bus sets rise and fall times; fall time counts as part of TLOW (wired-AND bus) and rise time lasts until a high is detected. TLOW, TSU;STO, TBUF, THD;STA and TSU;STA are timed by BAUD.BAUDLOW, or by BAUD.BAUD when BAUDLOW = 0; THIGH by BAUD.BAUD. TRISE depends on the bus impedance; TFALL on the bus impedance and the current limit of the open-drain output, and is usually taken as zero. Fm+ calls for a nominal high-to-low ratio of 1:2; BAUD and BAUDLOW may not both be zero. In smart mode the shortest time from an SDA change to the SCL rising edge after a DATA write is 6 APB cycles; a longer start-up time for slow rise times must be timed by software between the DATA write and the flag clear, and smart mode cannot then be used.

Writing the client address and direction to ADDR.ADDR starts a transaction; on a busy bus the host waits for idle, then sends a start and the address. Four outcomes follow. Arbitration lost or bus error: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.ARBLOST set (with STATUS.BUSERR for a bus error), SDA output is disabled and SCL released, and the host may do nothing until the bus is idle; STATUS.RXNACK keeps the last acknowledge received, and all flags clear on the next ADDR.ADDR write. No ACK: MB and RXNACK set with the clock held; the next step is a stop (preferred) or a repeated start; under SMBus a client must ACK its address, so no response means it is absent. Write, ACKed: MB sets and RXNACK clears with the clock held; software writes DATA.DATA, writes a new address (a repeated start is inserted) or sends a stop. Read, ACKed: the host receives the first byte, then INTFLAG.SB sets and RXNACK clears with the clock held; software acknowledges to read on (automatic in smart mode, ACK or NACK chosen by CTRLB.ACKACT), sends a new address or a stop.

After a successful write address, writing DATA.DATA sends a byte while the host watches for collisions; INTFLAG.MB sets either way, with STATUS.ARBLOST set on a lost arbitration or RXNACK cleared on an ACK. ARBLOST is best handled first in the MB interrupt, the same for address and data. RXNACK is checked after every byte, and after a NACK the host may not send more data. Receiving with SCLSM = 0: when SB sets one byte has arrived and the host must send ACK or NACK; if arbitration is lost while sending a NACK, MB sets instead of SB. Receiving with SCLSM = 1: when SB sets the byte has arrived and the ACK or NACK chosen by CTRLB.ACKACT has gone; ACKACT is set for the next bit, DATA read, and a command issued unless in smart mode.

A high-speed transfer starts with a host code 0b00001nnn sent at full speed (ADDR.ADDR with ADDR.HS = 0), which no client acknowledges; arbitration happens only in this phase. After the code and NACK the host write interrupt asserts and the client address is written with ADDR.HS = 1; the host then sends a repeated start and the address at high speed, and the bus stays in high speed until a stop. Each further repeated start needs ADDR.HS = 1 again with the new address. Needs CTRLA.SPEED = 0x2 and CTRLA.SCLSM = 1.

With ADDR.TENBITEN = 1, writing ADDR.ADDR sends two address bytes, which the client acknowledges; the first is sent with the direction bit (ADDR.ADDR[0]) 0 whether reading or writing. A NACK after the first byte raises the write interrupt with STATUS.RXNACK set; otherwise the write interrupt comes after the second byte. A read follows with a repeated start and the first address byte with direction 1. Procedure for a 10-bit read: write the address to ADDR.ADDR[10:1] with TENBITEN = 1 and ADDR.ADDR[0] = 0; at the Host on Bus interrupt write ADDR[7:0] = 11110 address[9:8] 1 with TENBITEN cleared; then transfer data.

The client is byte oriented and interrupt driven with an optional smart mode. With CTRLA.SCLSM = 0 the clock is held low either ahead of or behind the ACK bit. With SCLSM = 1 interrupts come only after the ACK is sent: on a host read the address and data interrupts arrive together after the address ACK; on a host write the first data interrupt comes after the first byte and its ACK. High-speed mode needs SCLSM = 1.

After a start the address packet is checked by the address logic; a mismatch is ignored until the next start. On a match INTFLAG.AMATCH sets and SCL is held low until software clears it, so response time is unlimited; with SCLSM = 1 the ACK or NACK chosen by CTRLB.ACKACT is sent before AMATCH sets. STATUS.DIR, updated only on a valid address, gives the direction. STATUS.COLL set means the last packet to this client collided; the lines were released silently, so the next AMATCH is the first sign (collisions follow the SMBus Address Resolution Protocol). Host read (DIR = 1): after an ACK, INTFLAG.DRDY sets to ask for transmit data; after a NACK the client waits for a new start and match. Host write (DIR = 0): after an ACK the client waits for data, a repeated start or a stop. CTRLB.CMD = 0x3 serves both directions, and writing 1 to INTFLAG.AMATCH also sends the ACK or NACK set by ACKACT.

After its address the client either waits for a byte or starts sending by writing DATA.DATA; INTFLAG.DRDY sets each time a byte is received or sent, and a received byte is acknowledged as CTRLB.ACKACT sets. Received: DRDY sets and SCL is held low until software acts. Sent: DRDY sets when the byte has gone; on a NACK (STATUS.RXNACK = 1) the client releases SDA and expects a stop or repeated start; a stop sets INTFLAG.PREC and the client returns to idle.

operation.topic: I2C client high-speed mode and 10-bit addressing
operation.text: With CTRLA.SPEED = 0x2 and SCLSM = 1 the client switches speed by itself: a start, host code and NACK put it in high speed and set STATUS.HS until the next stop. With ADDR.TENBITEN = 1 the two address bytes after a start are checked; the first is always acknowledged and the second raises the address flag. A write follows with N data bytes; a read follows with a repeated start and 11110 ADDR[9:8] 1, which raises a second address interrupt with DIR set, matched because of the 10-bit address before it.

With CTRLB.GCMD = 1 and 7-bit addressing, a stop sets INTFLAG.PREC if this client was addressed since the last stop; with GCMD = 0 a stop without an address match does not set PREC. A group command addresses several devices in one transmission, joined by repeated starts, ending in one stop; at the stop every client addressed starts executing its command, and this client's stop interrupt fires.

Three hardware SCL-low time-outs, timed by GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW, which must run from a 32 kHz oscillator, plus an SMBus-compatible SDA hold time. TTIMEOUT: one SCL low period of 25..35 ms (CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN). TLOW:SEXT: cumulative clock-low extension by a client of 25 ms over one message from start to stop (CTRLA.SEXTTOEN). TLOW:MEXT: cumulative clock-low extension by the host of 10 ms within any one byte, measured from a start or an ACK to the next ACK or stop (CTRLA.MEXTTOEN).

operation.topic: I2C smart mode, 4-wire mode and quick command
operation.text: In smart mode, reading DATA.DATA immediately sends the acknowledge selected in CTRLB.ACKACT. CTRLA.PINOUT = 1 selects 4-wire mode: the on-chip I2C output stages are left out of the path, SDA_OUT and SCL_OUT appear on PAD[2] and PAD[3], and reaching the bus then takes an outside I2C-compliant tri-state buffer. CTRLB.QCEN = 1 enables quick command: INTFLAG.SB or MB sets right after the client acknowledges its address, and software then sends a stop or a repeated start with CTRLB.CMD or ADDR.ADDR.

DMA needs smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN = 1). Client: an address match raises the address flag, and after it is serviced the data moves by DMA; RX is set when host-write data arrives and cleared by reading DATA, TX is set when a host read needs data and cleared by writing DATA. Host: ADDR is written with ADDR.ADDR, ADDR.LEN and ADDR.LENEN; with LENEN = 1, LEN sets the transaction length from 0 to 255 bytes, which DMA moves before an automatic NACK (on reads) and stop. A NACK on a host write before LEN bytes produces an automatic stop and sets STATUS.LENERR and INTFLAG.ERROR. Host RX is set when read data arrives (cleared by reading DATA), TX when write data is needed (cleared by writing DATA).

Client interrupts ERROR, DRDY, AMATCH and PREC, and host interrupts ERROR, SB and MB, are asynchronous and wake the device from any sleep mode; enabled ones read back from INTENSET or INTENCLR. No events. Host: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE runs in idle, and in standby too with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1; with RUNSTDBY = 0 it stops after the transaction in progress; any interrupt wakes the device. Client: RUNSTDBY = 1 lets Address Match wake the device; with RUNSTDBY = 0 all reception is dropped. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB.CMD, STATUS.BUSSTATE, ADDR.ADDR (host) and DATA (host) are synchronized.

The I2S is a bidirectional synchronous digital audio link compliant with the I2S bus specification, also serving TDM multi-slot codecs and PDM MEMS microphones. It has two clock units and two serializers, each enabled on its own, giving host, client and controller modes and receive or transmit. Pins are SDm, FSn, SCKn and MCKn, with n = 0, 1 the clock unit and m = 0, 1 the serializer; FSn is word select in I2S and frame sync in TDM. Each serializer has DMA, on one channel for all data or two channels for separate data channels, for continuous transfer to codecs, stereo DACs and ADCs, multi-slot TDM devices, mono or stereo PDM microphones, and single-channel bursts with a non-periodic frame sync. 8- and 16-bit compact stereo packs left and right samples into one word to halve DMA traffic. As host or controller it can output MCKn from 16×fs to 1024×fs for an external codec or DSP.

Data formats: 32-, 24-, 20-, 18-, 16- and 8-bit mono or stereo, and 16- and 8-bit compact stereo. Frame formats: two-channel I2S using word select; 1- to 8-slot TDM with frame sync and slots enabled one by one; 1- or 2-channel PDM reception; 1-channel burst with non-periodic frame sync. Two clock units can serve the serializers with one clock or with separate clocks, for sample rates including 32 kHz, 44.1 kHz, 48 kHz, 88.2 kHz, 96 kHz and 192 kHz. Host: data on internal clocks, with SCKn, MCKn and FSn output. Client: data on an external SCKn or MCKn. Controller: only MCKn, SCKn and FSn are output. Clock units and serializers enable separately; each serializer has DMA for receive or transmit; data holding register management keeps slots from mixing after an overrun or underrun.

The I2S pins are assigned to the peripheral function in PORT; only the inputs and outputs in use should be enabled, and unused ones stay free. The I2S runs in any sleep mode in which its source clocks run. CLK_I2S_APB comes from the PM, is off at reset, and should be turned off only after the I2S is disabled, or the I2S may freeze in an undefined state. GCLK_I2S_0 and GCLK_I2S_1 serve the two clock units, take a wide range of sources and frequencies, are used only in host and controller modes, and must be set up before use and before a software reset so that every clock domain resets. In host mode one clock unit can drive both serializers for synchronous transfers, or each serializer can use its own clock unit. DMA needs the DMAC, interrupts the NVIC; no events. It runs on while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless forced to halt. DATAm, INTFLAG and SYNCBUSY cannot be PAC write-protected.

Lines: SDm carries data for serializer m, SCKn the serial clock of clock unit n, FSn the frame sync or word select marking each frame start, and optionally MCKn an oversampling clock for a codec. A frame starts on the active frame-sync edge and holds 1 to 8 slots of 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits, each carrying one sample of 8, 16, 18, 20, 24 or 32 bits; the frame period is 1/fs. Mono (SERCTRLm.MONO = 1): on transmit, left-channel data is repeated on the right; on receive, right-channel data is dropped and left-channel data copied to the right; in TDM with more than two slots, each even slot is copied into the next odd slot, both ways. In 2-channel I2S, one or two slots are set and successive words alternate left and right by the polarity of FSn; one slot suffices for compact stereo, and 32-bit slots allow two. TDM takes up to 8 slots (4 slots, 4 words a frame). PDM delivers a 1-bit sample on SDI at every rising and falling edge of SCKn. Burst mode, for control data as with a DSP, starts one transfer at each 1-bit-wide frame-sync pulse, sent only when a transfer is requested.

The two serializers share one clock unit or use one each. Before enabling, write CLKCTRLn and SERCTRLm; in host mode also set a GCLK_I2S to the needed frequency, with CLKCTRLn.NBSLOTS slots per frame, CLKCTRLn.SLOTSIZE bits per slot and fSCKn = fs × slots × bits per slot. Then set CTRLA.CKENn, CTRLA.SERENm and CTRLA.ENABLE. A clock unit may be enabled alone (controller mode) to output MCKn, SCKn and FSn; serializers need their clock unit enabled. Clearing CKENn or SERENm stops a unit once pending transmit frames finish, or, when receiving, once the current slot is complete. Example for fs = 48 kHz and MCKn = 384×fs (18.432 MHz): run the generic clock at 18.432 MHz with CLKCTRLn.MCKOUTDIV = 0x0; with 6 slots (NBSLOTS = 0x5) of 32 bits (SLOTSIZE = 0x3) SCKn is 48 kHz × 6 × 32 = 9.216 MHz, obtained with CLKCTRLn.MCKDIV = 0x1; without MCKn the generic clock can be 9.216 MHz with MCKDIV = 0x0.

Receive: read DATAm whenever INTFLAG.RXRDYm is set; successive reads give left then right, or in TDM the first slot to the last (NBSLOTS sets how many). Transmit: write DATAm whenever INTFLAG.TXRDYm is set, in the same order. The flags can be polled, raise interrupts through INTENSET, or trigger DMA: four DMAC triggers, I2S RX 0, I2S RX 1, I2S TX 0 and I2S TX 1 (named I2S_DMAC_ID_RX_m, I2S_DMAC_ID_TX_m), each moving one word whenever its ready flag sets.

Client: SCKn and FSn are inputs driven by an external host, and no generic clock is needed. Host: MCKn, SCKn and FSn are outputs generated from GCLK_I2S_n under CLKCTRLn, some codecs needing MCKn at a multiple of fs such as 256×fs. Controller: only CTRLA and CLKCTRLn are set (divisions, slot count, slot size, frame sync, clock enable). CLKCTRLn.MCKEN = 1 puts GCLK_I2S_n on MCKn, divided as set by MCKSEL and MCKOUTDIV. With MCKSEL and SCKSEL both 0, SCKn is GCLK_I2S_n divided by MCKDIV + 1. Without MCKn the generic clock can serve directly as SCKn (MCKDIV = 0); if its frequency is a multiple of SCKn, MCKDIV divides it down.

Each serializer has one DATAm register for all slots. Receive: a new word sets INTFLAG.RXRDYm, cleared by reading DATAm; a word arriving before the previous one is read is an overrun and sets INTFLAG.RXORm, cleared by writing 1. Transmit: an empty DATAm sets INTFLAG.TXRDYm, cleared by writing; a word needed before it is written is an underrun and sets INTFLAG.TXURm, cleared by writing 1. On underrun SERCTRLm.TXSAME = 0 sends a zero word and TXSAME = 1 repeats the last word of that slot.

operation.topic: I2S host, controller and client modes
operation.text: Host and controller drive the serial clock and word select or frame sync, plus a host clock if wanted; a controller keeps its serializers off and only clocks are output for outside receivers and transmitters. In client mode SCKn and FSn are inputs from an external host.

Data is left-adjusted in the word-select slot, MSB first, starting one clock after the word-select transition; bits change on the falling edge of SCK and are sampled on the rising edge. Word select is low for the left channel and high for the right. 16-bit compact stereo: CLKCTRL0.SLOTSIZE = 0x1, NBSLOTS = 0x1, SERCTRL0.DATASIZE = 0x05, CLKCTRLn.BITDELAY = 0x01 (1-bit delay from frame sync), CLKCTRLn.FSWIDTH = 0x01 (half frame). 24-bit stereo transmitter in 24-bit slots: SLOTSIZE = 0x2, NBSLOTS = 0x1, DATASIZE = 0x01, BITDELAY = 0x01, FSWIDTH = 0x01. SERCTRLm.DATASIZE sets the word length to 8, 16, 18, 20, 24 or 32 bits; when the slot is longer, bits are added as SERCTRLm.EXTEND sets, and when it is shorter the extra bits are not sent or the received word is extended per EXTEND.

A TDM frame carries CLKCTRLn.NBSLOTS + 1 slots. CLKCTRLn.FSWIDTH and FSINV set the frame-sync width and polarity; SERCTRLm sets left or right adjustment in the slot, MSB or LSB first, and whether data starts at the FSn transition or one clock later. Bits change on the falling edge of SCK and are sampled on the rising edge. FSn marks the start of slot 0; CLKCTRLn.BITDELAY sets the delay from frame start to the first bit; FSWIDTH sets the frame-sync width: BIT is a single SCKn period, SLOT a whole slot, HALF half the frame. NBSLOTS sets the slot count, SLOTSIZE the bits per slot, SERCTRLm.DATASIZE the word length (8, 16, 18, 20, 24 or 32 bits), and SERCTRLm.EXTEND the fill when slot and word lengths differ.

A PDM microphone gives a 1-bit sample on SDI at each rising edge of SCKn; a second (right) microphone is set to drive data on each falling edge. One microphone: normal receive mode, one slot, 16- or 32-bit data size, so each word holds 16 or 32 samples. Two microphones: PDM2 mode, one slot, 32-bit data size; each word holds 16 samples of each, left in the lower half and right in the upper half, as in compact stereo. SCKn is set to the microphone's oversampling frequency through GCLK_I2S_n and CLKCTRLn.MCKDIV: fs = 48 kHz with fo = 64 × fs needs SCKn at 3.072 MHz. Only SCKn and SDIn are used. PDM2 settings: SLOTSIZE = 0x01 (16 bits), NBSLOTS = 0x01 (2 slots), SERCTRL0.DATASIZE = 0x00 (32-bit).

Received words pass through a receive formatting unit before reaching the data holding register, and words written for transmission through a transmit formatting unit. SERCTRLm sets the options: SLOTADJ (left or right justified in the slot), BITREV (bit reversal), WORDADJ (left or right justified in the data word) and EXTEND (extension to the word size).

SERCTRLm.DMA connects a serializer to one DMAC channel, or to one per slot parity in stereo. The DMAC reads or writes DATAm for all slots in turn, using 32-, 16- or 8-bit transfers according to SERCTRLm.DATASIZE; compact stereo moves by 16-bit transfers for 8-bit samples and 32-bit transfers for 16-bit samples. Interrupts RXRDYm, RXORm, TXRDYm and TXURm are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode; each has an INTFLAG flag with INTENSET and INTENCLR bits, all are ORed into one NVIC request, and INTFLAG tells which fired. No events.

The I2S runs in every sleep mode that keeps its clocks. A synchronized operation sets its SYNCBUSY bit at once until done; starting another one while that bit is 1 is a peripheral bus error. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.CKENx and CTRLA.SERENx are synchronized (SYNCBUSY.SWRST, ENABLE, CKENx, SERENx); DATAn is read-synchronized when serializer n receives and write-synchronized when it transmits (SYNCBUSY.DATAn). For testing, SERCTRLm.RXLOOP = 1 joins the other serializer's transmit output to serializer m's receive input inside the chip (SERCTRL0.RXLOOP = 1: SD1 output to SD0 input; SERCTRL1.RXLOOP = 1: SD0 output to SD1 input); serializer m must be a receiver and the other a transmitter. RXLOOP = 0 restores the SDm pin. Serializer m is disabled before SERCTRLm is written.

Audio: the I2S drives SCKn, FSn (word select) and serial data out to an external I2S receiver; left and right words alternate, MSB first. Time slot: MCKn, SCKn and FSn go to two external audio codecs, each using its own time slot of the frame, with serial data out (SDO) and serial data in (SDI) shared. Codec: MCKn, SCKn and FSn to one external codec, with SDO and SDI, the codec using the first slot. PDM microphones: SCKn at 64 fs clocks two external PDM microphones whose data share SDI; the left-channel microphone has L/RSEL tied to VDD and the right-channel one to GND, and SDI carries right and left samples alternately.

Up to five 16-bit timer/counters, each made of a counter, a prescaler, two compare/capture channels and control logic. Each works as an 8-bit or 16-bit TC with two channels, or two TCs pair into one 32-bit TC with two channels. The counter counts prescaled clock ticks or events. It generates frequencies and single-slope PWM, and captures events, frequency and pulse width by timestamping input events. It has one input event, interrupts and output events on overflow/underflow and on compare match or capture, an internal prescaler, and DMA requests.

Pins are assigned in PORT. The TC runs in any sleep mode in which its clock runs; its interrupts wake the device and its events act through the event system without waking it. CLK_TCx_APB is masked in the PM. From TC3 on, the instances pair even and odd on one generic clock GCLK_TCx, so both of a pair use the same clock; it is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register accesses are synchronized. DMA needs the DMAC, interrupts the NVIC; events go to the event system. The TC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. INTFLAG, STATUS, READREQ, COUNT, PER and CCx cannot be PAC write-protected.

The counter counts event-system events or GCLK_TCx ticks through the prescaler, up or down, and is compared continuously with TOP or ZERO and with each CCx; matches can request DMA, raise interrupts or send events, and in waveform modes set the period or pulse width. COUNT and CCx are 8, 16 or 32 bits with the matching MAX; 8-bit mode adds a period register PER. Range and clock set the finest time resolution. Capture measures period and pulse width or timestamps chosen edges of an internal event.

CTRLA (except RUNSTDBY, ENABLE and SWRST) and EVCTRL.EVACT are enable-protected; enable-protected CTRLA bits may be written in the same write that sets ENABLE but not in the one that clears it. Steps: enable CLK_TCx_APB; choose 8-, 16- or 32-bit mode in CTRLA.MODE (16-bit by default); choose CTRLA.WAVEGEN; optionally prescale with CTRLA.PRESCALER and pick CTRLA.PRESYNC; CTRLBSET.ONESHOT = 1 for one-shot; CTRLBSET.DIR = 1 to count down from TOP; CTRLC.CPTEN for capture channels; CTRLC.INVEN to invert outputs or pin inputs. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables the TC; disable the TC before a reset.

GCLK_TCx feeds a prescaler counter whose output toggles at the selected value; outputs from 1 to 1/1024 are available (GCLK_TC divided by 1, 2, 4, 8, 64, 256 or 1024). Above 1, CTRLA.PRESYNC sets whether the counter updates on the next GCLK_TCx or the next prescaled clock. Counting events bypasses the prescaler; prescaled ticks and event ticks together form CLK_TC_CNT. COUNT8 has its own PER register for the top value; COUNT16, the default, has none; COUNT32 pairs TC4 with TC5 or TC6 with TC7 (TC3 has no 32-bit mode), set up through the even TC's registers while the odd one is a client with STATUS.SLAVE set, whose own registers do not reflect or affect the 32-bit counter and whose COUNT and CCx are not accessed normally.

Counting up, the counter wraps from TOP to zero on the next tick (overflow, INTFLAG.OVF); counting down, from zero to TOP (underflow). CTRLB.DIR = 0 counts up, 1 counts down; the direction may change while running. EVCTRL.OVFEO = 1 gives an event on overflow or underflow. In one-shot mode counting stops after the wrap. COUNT may be written while running, and a write beats count, clear and reload; on start COUNT is ZERO or TOP by direction unless written or stopped elsewhere. Stop (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x2) holds the count, clears all waveforms and sets STATUS.STOP. Re-trigger (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x1, or EVCTRL.EVACT = 0x1) reloads or clears the counter by direction while counting, or resumes from COUNT when stopped; with the re-trigger event action, enabling does not start the counter: the next event starts it and each later event restarts it. Count action (EVACT = 0x2) steps the counter on each event by direction. Start action (EVACT = 0x3) starts a stopped counter on an event and does nothing while counting; once enabled, the counter starts on the event or a software re-trigger.

Channels default to compare. For a waveform on a pin: choose CTRLA.WAVEGEN, optionally invert with CTRLC.INVx, and assign the pin in PORT. A match between COUNT and CCx sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TC_CNT, with an interrupt (INTENSET.MCx) and/or event (EVCTRL.MCEOx). Four modes: NFRQ (normal frequency), MFRQ (match frequency), NPWM (normal PWM) and MPWM (match PWM). In NFRQ and NPWM, TOP is PER in 8-bit mode (changed by writing PER) and fixed at MAX in 16- and 32-bit modes. NFRQ: the period is PER (8-bit) or MAX, and WO[x] toggles on each match with CCx. MFRQ: CC0 sets the period and WO[0] toggles on each update. NPWM is single-slope: counting up, WO[x] is set at start or at TOP and cleared at the CCx match; counting down, cleared at start or at ZERO and set at the CCx match. MPWM: CC0 sets the period and CC1 drives WO[1]; each overflow/underflow puts a one-clock negative pulse on WO[0].

The period changes by writing a new TOP to PER or CC0, by mode. Written while counting down close to zero, the old TOP may be reloaded because of synchronization delay, giving one extra cycle before the new TOP takes effect. COUNT and TOP compare continuously, so a TOP written below the current COUNT makes the counter run on to wrap before matching; without buffering this wraparound can happen in any mode when counting up.

Capture needs EVCTRL.TCEI = 1 (the event input) and the channel's CTRLC.CPTENx bit set. RETRIGGER, COUNT and START act only on event-system events; period and duty cycle of a pin can be captured through the EIC and the event system. Event capture timestamps each event into the channel. A new capture while INTFLAG.MCx is still set is a capture overflow: the timestamp is dropped and INTFLAG.ERR sets. Period and pulse-width capture takes two captures and restarts the counter on one edge: EVCTRL.EVACT = PWP captures the period T into CC1 and the pulse width tp into CC0, and EVACT = PPW captures T into CC0 and tp into CC1; EVCTRL.TCINV = 1 moves the wrap to the falling edge. CTRLC.CPTEN = 0x3 captures on both CC0 and CC1; if one measurement is enough the other channel is free.

With CTRLBSET.ONESHOT = 1 the counter stops at the next overflow or underflow, sets STATUS.STOP and drives the waveform outputs to zero; CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT turns it off. A software re-trigger, re-trigger event or start event restarts it and clears STATUS.STOP.

DMA OVF is set on an update (overflow or underflow) and cleared on the next clock cycle. DMA MCx is set on each compare match and cleared on the next clock cycle for a compare channel; for a capture channel it is set while CCx holds valid data and cleared when CCx is read. With the OVF request the new value lands after the update, after DMA and synchronization delay, so a COUNT that has already passed the new value by the time PER or CCx changes gives no match. With the MCx request, writing a CCx below COUNT when counting down, or above it when counting up, can match again before the overflow, triggering the next transfer and dropping the previous value from WO[x]. Interrupts OVF, MCx, ERR and SYNCRDY share one request line; INTFLAG tells which. Output events OVF and MC (enabled by EVCTRL.MCEOx); input actions selected by EVCTRL.EVACT: start, re-trigger, increment or decrement, count, and period capture (PPW and PWP); EVCTRL.TCEI enables the input. The TC takes asynchronous event inputs only.

The TC can run in any sleep mode; standby needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1. It wakes the device by interrupt from any sleep mode or acts through the event system. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE are synchronized, and CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, CTRLC, COUNT, PER and CCx are synchronized both when written and when read.

Up to four timer/counters for control applications, TCC[0:3], each a counter, prescaler, compare/capture channels and control logic, counting events or clock pulses, timestamping input events to capture frequency and pulse width, and generating frequencies and PWM. Waveform extensions for motor control, ballast, LED, H-bridge and power converters give low- and high-side outputs with optional dead time and synchronized bit patterns across the outputs; fault options shut external drivers down safely and predictably. Some instances have fewer channels and features.

Up to four compare/capture channels with double-buffered period and compare/capture and circular buffers on period and compare registers. Waveforms: frequency, single-slope PWM, and dual-slope PWM with half-cycle reload. Capture: event, frequency and pulse width. Extensions: configurable distribution of channel outputs across pins, low- and high-side outputs with programmable dead time, double-buffered swap and pattern generation, and dithering. Fault protection: two recoverable and two non-recoverable fault sources, the debugger able to be a non-recoverable source. Events: two counter inputs (EVx) and one input per channel (MCx); outputs Count, Re-Trigger and Overflow, and one compare match/capture output per channel. Interrupts on overflow and re-trigger, compare match/capture and faults. DMA requests.

Pins are assigned in PORT. The TCC runs in any sleep mode in which its clock runs, wakes the device by interrupt, and acts through events without waking it. CLK_TCCx_APB is masked in the PM; GCLK_TCCx clocks the TCC and must be set up in GCLK first; TCC0 and TCC1 share one generic clock generator. GCLK_TCCx is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA needs the DMAC, interrupts the NVIC; events go to the event system. The TCC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. INTFLAG, STATUS, PER, PERB, CCx, CCBx, WAVE, WAVEB, PATT and PATTB cannot be PAC write-protected.

Each TCC has up to four channels CCx. COUNT, PER with its buffer PERB, and CCx with buffers CCBx are 16 or 24 bits, depending on the instance; each buffer has a buffer-valid flag. COUNT is compared continuously with TOP and ZERO, raising interrupts, DMA requests or events, and setting period and pulse width in waveform modes. A prescaled GCLK_TCCx and event-system events drive the counter; events also feed capture. The recoverable fault unit acts on the channel outputs from events, restarting or halting the period, shortening the active pulse or disabling the output while the fault lasts, as for current-sense regulation and zero-crossing or demagnetization re-triggering; it shares the MCE0 and MCE1 asynchronous events, uses only asynchronous events, and can filter, blank and qualify its inputs against glitches. Some instances add a chain of optional units: the two kinds of fault handling, then OTMX, DTI, SWAP and the pattern generator. The output matrix (OTMX) routes the waveforms across pins in several arrangements. Dead-time insertion (DTI) turns each of the four lowest OTMX outputs into a pair, LS (same sense) and HS (inverted), with an optional dead time between their edges. SWAP exchanges LS and HS, for fast-decay motor control. Pattern generation sets outputs to fixed levels at UPDATE, for stepper motors and full bridges. The non-recoverable fault unit forces the outputs to a preset safe state on a fault event, for instant shutdown of high-current or high-voltage drives; it shares TCE0 and TCE1 and, unfiltered, acts asynchronously even with no clock.

Enable-protected: CTRLA (except RUNSTDBY, ENABLE and SWRST), FCTRLA and FCTRLB, WEXCTRL, DRVCTRL and EVCTRL; enable-protected CTRLA bits may be written together with setting ENABLE but not with clearing it. Steps: enable CLK_TCCx_APB; for capture set CTRLA.CPTEN. Optional: CTRLA.PRESCALER and PRESCSYNC; CTRLBSET.DIR = 1 to count down; WAVE.WAVEGEN; WAVE.POL; DRVCTRL.INVEN to invert outputs per channel. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables the TCC; disable it before a reset.

GCLK_TCCx feeds a prescaler with outputs from 1 to 1/1024 (divide by 1, 2, 4, 8, 64, 256 or 1024); above 1, CTRLA.PRESYNC chooses update on the next GCLK_TCC or next prescaled clock. Counting events bypasses the prescaler; prescaled and event ticks form CLK_TCC_COUNT. Each tick clears, reloads, increments or decrements the counter by mode; a clear or reload ends one counter cycle. CTRLB.DIR = 0 counts up: at TOP the next tick sets zero (overflow) and INTFLAG.OVF; DIR = 1 counts down: at ZERO the counter reloads TOP (underflow) and OVF sets. OVF can trigger an interrupt, DMA or event; with CTRLBSET.ONESHOT the counter stops there. COUNT may be written while running and a write beats count, clear and reload; on start COUNT is ZERO or TOP by direction unless written or stopped elsewhere; direction may change while running.

Stop (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x2): the counter holds its value, waveforms go to the state set by DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx, STATUS.STOP sets. Pause: with EVCTRL.EVACT1 = 0x3 (STOP) an event stops the counter at once with outputs held, until a start event (EVACT0 = 0x3). Re-trigger (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x1, or EVACTn = 0x1): reloads or clears by direction while counting and sets INTFLAG.TRG, with an event if EVCTRL.TRGEO = 1; resumes from COUNT when stopped; with this event action, enabling does not start the counter, the next event starts it and each later one restarts it. Start (EVACT0 = 0x3): starts a stopped counter, no effect while counting; enabling does not start the counter, the next event does, and later events do not restart it. Count (EVACT0 = 0x5): steps by direction per event. Direction (EVACT1 = 0x2): the event level, on an asynchronous event path, overrides and updates the direction bit. Increment (EVACT0 = 0x4, INC): TCE0 increments whatever the direction. Decrement (EVACT1 = 0x4, DEC): TCE1 decrements whatever the direction. Non-recoverable fault (EVACTn = 0x7): stops the counter and overrides the outputs per DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx; TCE0 and TCE1 must be asynchronous. Off (EVACTn = 0x0): enabling also starts the counter.

Channels default to compare. CCBx double-buffers CCx, loading it at UPDATE or on a forced update (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x3) so pulses stay symmetric and glitch free. For a pin waveform choose WAVE.WAVEGEN, optionally invert with DRVCTRL.INVENx, and assign the pin in PORT. A COUNT-CCx match sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TCC_COUNT, with interrupt (INTENSET.MCx), event (EVCTRL.MCEOx), both, and a DMA request. Seven modes: NFRQ, MFRQ, NPWM, and dual-slope DSTOP (interrupt/event at TOP), DSBOTTOM (at ZERO), DSBOTH (at TOP and ZERO) and DSCRITICAL (critical, at ZERO). TOP is CC0 in MFRQ and PER in every other mode. Dual-slope modes update when the counter reaches ZERO; the others update on wraparound, overflow, underflow or re-trigger.

NFRQ: PER sets the period and WO[x] toggles on each COUNT-CCx match, setting the channel's match flag. MFRQ: CC0 sets the period and WO[0] toggles on each update. NPWM is single-slope: TOP sets the period and CCx the duty cycle; counting up, WO[x] is set at start or at TOP and cleared at the CCx match; counting down, cleared at start or at ZERO and set at the CCx match.

PER sets TOP and CCx the duty cycle; the counter runs ZERO to PER and back. WO[x] is set on the match while counting up and cleared on the match while counting down. Interrupts and events come at TOP (counting up) and/or ZERO. DSBOTH needs the circular buffer enabled for the update at TOP. Dual slope reaches a lower top frequency than single slope; TOP sets the resolution, at least 1 bit (TOP = 0x00000001), and the output reaches at most half the TCC clock with TOP = 0x00000001 and no prescaling. In DSTOP, DSBOTTOM and DSBOTH with TOP below MAX/2, the CCx MSB picks the ramp on which the match interrupt or event fires (rising for 0, falling for 1). Dual-slope critical mode makes non-aligned centred pulses: PER sets the period, CCx sets the output edge while counting up and CC(x + CC_NUM/2) the edge while counting down.
WAVE.POLx applies in every waveform mode. In single- and dual-slope PWM it flips the pulse alignment to the start or end of the cycle per channel; in NFRQ and MFRQ it is the output's initial state.

operation.topic: TCC double buffering and period changes
operation.text: PATT, WAVE, PER and CCx are double buffered, each with a buffer-valid bit in STATUS (PATTBV, WAVEBV, PERBV, CCBVx). With a valid buffer and CTRLB.LUPD = 0 (cleared by writing CTRLBCLR.LUPD = 1) the buffers load into the registers at hardware UPDATE and the valid bits clear; the software update command (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x3) works whatever LUPD is. Registers and buffers are both in the register map, so buffering is optional; CTRLBSET.LUPD = 1 turns it off. In NFRQ, MFRQ or PWM counting down with buffering on, PERB is copied into PER continuously regardless of update. Any write to PER or CCx takes effect after the synchronization delay. Unbuffered, a TOP written below COUNT while counting up makes the counter run on to wrap before matching, in any mode; with buffering the buffer may be written at any time and PER updates only at the update condition, so no wraparound or odd waveform occurs.

Capture needs EVCTRL.MCEIx = 1 and the channel's CTRLA.CPTENx set. Event capture timestamps event-system events. CCBx and CCx act as a FIFO: whenever CCx is empty or read, CCBx moves into it and its valid flag sets the channel interrupt flag with optional interrupt, event or DMA request; CCBx cannot be read, so all data is read from CCx. A capture while STATUS.CCBV is still set is a capture overflow: dropped, with INTFLAG.ERR set. Period and pulse-width capture: EVCTRL.EVACT1 = PPW captures T into CC0 and tp into CC1; PWP captures T into CC1 and tp into CC0; one capture on each edge, with EVCTRL.TCEINVx = 1 moving the wrap to the falling edge. A channel not in capture mode ignores the action and stays a compare channel; an unused one is free. A capture while INTFLAG.MCx is still set is dropped with ERR set. With FCTRLn.CAPTURE = CAPTMIN and up-counting, a count of 0 is never captured; the whole range including 0 needs down-counting. In dual-slope PWM with TOP below MAX/2, the CCx MSB records CTRLB.DIR to show the ramp (0 rising, 1 falling).

One-shot (CTRLBSET.ONESHOT = 1, cleared by CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT) stops the counter at the next overflow or underflow, sets STATUS.STOP and drives the outputs to the values set by DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx; a software re-trigger, re-trigger event or start event restarts it and clears STOP. PER and CC0 to CC3 support circular buffering: at each update the register value is copied into its buffer. It serves RAMP2, RAMP2A and DSBOTH.

Dithering adds extra clock cycles to some compare matches, one at a time by a blue-noise sequence that limits flicker, over a frame of 16, 32 or 64 PWM cycles, refining the average pulse width or period. CTRLA.RESOLUTION selects DITH4 (16 frames), DITH5 (32) or DITH6 (64). In COUNT, PER and CCx a DITHERCY field (the low 4 bits in DITH4) give the extra cycles per frame and the remaining bits the compare value. An extra cycle is added in a given cycle when ((MASK & (cycle × dithercy)) + dithercy) > MASK, with MASK = 0x0f, 0x1f or 0x3f for DITH4, DITH5 or DITH6. Dithering the pulse width leaves the period unchanged.

All three run in single-slope PWM, chosen by WAVE.RAMP. RAMP1 is the default single-slope PWM. RAMP2 modes, for power factor correction, half-bridge and push-pull SMPS, interleave two counter cycles: in cycle A the odd channel output is off, in cycle B the even one; the ramp index changes at each update and CTRLBSET.IDXCMD can change it. RAMP2: PER sets the A and B periods, different per ramp with WAVE.CIPEREN = 1; two channels make two outputs, or one output with the other channel capturing. RAMP2A: as RAMP2, but with the circular buffer on, CC0 drives both WO[0] and WO[1] with the same polarity, leaving channel 1 free to capture. RAMP2C: no circular-buffer update limits; CC0 sets ramp A's period and PER ramp B's; with more than two channels WO[0] is set by CC2 (high) and CC0 (low); with two channels and WAVE.POL0 = 0 a pulse on WO[0] lasts all of ramp A. Faults: Fault A can re-trigger, and WO[1] can be kept on Fault B.

Fault A and Fault B can restart or halt the counter and act on CC0 and CC1, clamping their outputs inactive while the fault lasts or from the first valid fault to the end of the cycle. The first two channel input events, TCCxMC0 and TCCxMC1, are the Fault A and B inputs; their event channels must be asynchronous, and the TCC must run a PWM mode. Each input has three filters, used alone or together, set in FCTRLA and FCTRLB. Input filtering: detection is asynchronous by default and acts even where the clock is off; FCTRLn.FILTERVAL discards events shorter than FILTERVAL clocks and delays valid ones by FILTERVAL clocks. Blanking (FCTRLn.BLANK edge choice, FCTRLn.BLANKVAL duration) ignores the input for a time after a chosen output edge, against bounce. Maximum blanking (BLANKVAL = 255) is 2.67 µs without prescaler or 170 µs with prescaling at fGCLK_TCCx = 96 MHz, and 170 µs or 10.9 ms at 1 MHz. Qualification (FCTRLn.QUAL = 1) disables the input whenever its channel output is inactive.

Actions are set per fault and can be combined. Keep (FCTRLn.KEEP = 1): the channel output is clamped to zero while the fault lasts and released at the start of the first cycle after it ends. Restart (FCTRLn.RESTART = 1): the cycle stops and a new one starts as soon as the fault appears; in RAMP1 the outputs stay inactive while the fault lasts; in RAMP2 the new cycle changes the cycle index, and Fault A is qualified only in cycle A and Fault B only in cycle B. Hardware halt (FCTRLn.HALT = 0x1): the counter halts and the cycle stretches while the fault lasts, channel 0 output held inactive; counting resumes when the fault ends (with restart also on, the counter restarts then; in RAMP2 and RAMP2A a new cycle changes the index). Software halt (HALT = 0x2): as hardware halt, but restarting also needs software to clear the FAULTn bit in STATUS after the fault ends.

FCTRLn.CAPTURE captures the counter when the fault occurs. CAPT: standard capture, interrupt on every capture. CAPTMIN and CAPTMAX: CCx keeps the lowest or highest timestamp; a capture happens only when the count is below (CAPTMIN) or above (CAPTMAX) the last captured value, and MCx sets on each new absolute minimum or maximum. LOCMIN and LOCMAX: CCx follows the count at each fault and MCx sets when the value is above or equal (LOCMIN) or below or equal (LOCMAX) the previous one, marking a local minimum or maximum. DERIV0: the OR of LOCMIN and LOCMAX, notifying each local extreme. Before CAPTMIN, CCx must be set to a value other than zero, and before CAPTMAX to a value other than top, or that channel never captures. Outside CAPT, interrupts come only on extreme values.

A non-recoverable fault forces every compare output to the level set in DRVCTRL.NRE and DRVCTRL.NRV. The fault inputs EV0 and EV1 are enabled in EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1. DRVCTRL.FILTERVALn adds a digital filter against glitches, making detection synchronous and delaying the action by the filter value in clocks. With DBGCTRL.FDDBD = 1, entering debug raises a non-recoverable debug fault state and its interrupt (DFS). In RAMP2, RAMP2A or DSBOTH with CTRLBSET.LUPD = 1, a change of ramp index or count direction raises a non-recoverable update fault state and its interrupt (UFS).
