Behind the recoverable fault stage sit four optional units, in order OTMX (routing), DTI (dead time), SWAP and the pattern generator. DTI and SWAP work in slices, slice x acting on the pin pair WO[x] and WO[WO_NUM/2 + x]. OTMX configuration 0x0, the default, routes channel n to OTMX[n] and repeats the channels modulo their number on extra outputs (CC0 again at OTMX[CC_NUM]). 0x1 repeats modulo half the channel count, giving the lower channels twice the outputs, so two channels can drive the four transistors of a full bridge, with pattern generation overriding outputs for every quadrant. 0x2 puts CC0 on every pin, for a stepper motor with pattern generation. 0x3 puts CC0 on the first output and CC1 on all others, which with pattern generation and the fault extension serves a boost stage feeding as many as seven LED strings.

operation.topic: TCC dead-time insertion and pattern generation
operation.text: DTI holds both outputs low for a dead time at each transition, so LS (the non-inverted copy) and HS (the inverted copy) never switch at once. Four identical generators serve channels 0 to 3, sharing one dead-time register set that holds separate low-side and high-side values. An 8-bit counter counts down one per peripheral clock to zero, forcing both outputs off while non-zero; a rising OTMX output reloads it from DTLS and a falling one from DTHS. The pattern generator drives a synchronized bit pattern across its pins, for BLDC commutation, stepper motors and full bridges; PATT is double buffered (PGEB, PGVB) and loads at UPDATE, or PATT.PGE and PATT.PGV can be written directly when no synchronization is needed.

OVF request: each cycle with an update (overflow, underflow or re-trigger), cleared by hardware on DMA acknowledge. MCx compare: set only on a compare match, cleared on acknowledge. MCx capture: set while CCx holds valid data, cleared when CCx is read. Circular buffers (RAMP2, RAMP2A and DSBOTH only) need their buffers written in order and in step with the timer updates, which the DMA triggers ensure. In RAMP2 and RAMP2A a circular channel's request comes at the start of ramp B instead of at a match, and with any circular buffer on, the OVF request comes at the start of ramp A, after a DMA transfer in the previous ramp B; one DMA channel on the MC trigger refreshes the ramp A values and a second on OVF the ramp B values. In DSBOTH a circular channel's request comes at the start of down-counting and OVF at the start of up-counting, after a transfer in the previous down-count; the MC-triggered channel updates values while counting up and the OVF-triggered one while counting down.

Interrupt sources OVF, TRG, CNT (see EVCTRL.CNTSEL), ERR, UFS, DFS, FAULTn (recoverable), FAULTx (non-recoverable) and MCx are asynchronous wake-up sources and share one request line; INTFLAG tells which. Output events OVF, TRG, CNT and MCx, each enabled by its EVCTRL.xxEO bit. Channel input events (MCx) capture or raise a recoverable or non-recoverable fault. Event 1 (TCCx EV1): re-trigger, direction control, stop, decrement, period and pulse-width capture, or non-recoverable fault. Event 0 (TCCx EV0): re-trigger, count by direction, start on the event's rising edge (later events do not restart it; it counts on the prescaled GCLK_TCCx to TOP or ZERO), increment regardless of direction, count on each prescaled clock while an asynchronous event is active, or non-recoverable fault. EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1 choose the actions and EVCTRL.MCEIx and TCEIx enable inputs; with several events connected, the action applies to each.

The TCC can run in any sleep mode; standby needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1; it wakes the device by interrupt or acts through events in any sleep mode. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE, and to CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, STATUS, PATT, PATTB, WAVE, COUNT, PER, PERB, CCx and CCBx, are synchronized. Reads of CTRLBCLR and CTRLBSET are synchronized; COUNT is read-synchronized on demand with the READSYNC command (CTRLBSET.CMD).

A USB 2.1 compliant interface that works as a device or as an embedded host, at full speed (12 Mbit/s) or low speed (1.5 Mbit/s), with Link Power Management (LPM-L1). The transceivers, their pull-up and pull-down resistors and the series resistors are on the chip. As a device it has 8 endpoint addresses, each with an IN and an OUT endpoint (16 in all), each settable to control, interrupt, bulk or isochronous transfers; as a host it has 8 physical pipes. Data payloads can be up to 1023 bytes, and neither endpoints nor pipes have size limits. Endpoint configuration and data buffers live in system SRAM, placed where software chooses and sized by how many endpoints are in use; a DMA built into the USB moves the data itself, with no CPU or DMAC work. Every endpoint and pipe supports multi-packet transfers and dual banks. Device mode also supports feedback endpoints and crystal-less clocking; host mode supports phase-locked SOFs and several virtual pipes multiplexed on one physical pipe, allowing an unlimited USB tree. A 1 kHz SOF clock can be put out on a pin. When the bus is idle and suspended the MCU can sleep in any mode, and bus resume wakes it from any mode.

operation.topic: USB pins, power, clocks and dependencies
operation.text: DM, DP and the 1 kHz SOF output (available in device and host mode) are given to the USB through PORT first. The USB keeps running in any sleep mode where its clock source runs, and its interrupts wake the device. The bus clock CLK_USB_AHB is gated in the main clock module; the generic clock GCLK_USB must be set up in GCLK before use and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register writes are synchronized. GCLK_USB must be 48 MHz ± 0.25 % for low and full speed, and CLK_USB_AHB at least 8 MHz to keep up with 12 Mbit/s full speed. A digital PLL inside the USB recovers the bus clock and meets the USB jitter specification; crystal-less device operation uses the USB clock recovery module. The interrupt line goes to the NVIC; there are no events. The USB keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except the device INTFLAG, EPINTFLAG, host INTFLAG and PINTFLAG registers; PAC protection does not apply to debugger accesses.

The DP/DM output drivers are trimmed by production calibration values that software copies from the NVM software calibration area into PADCAL before enabling the USB; without them the specified accuracy is not met. After reset the USB is idle: disabled, its clock stopped, the pad suspended and the device and host state reset. CTRLA.MODE (device or host) and CTRLB.SPDCONF (speed) are written first and take effect when CTRLA.ENABLE is set, which puts the USB into device or host mode; clearing CTRLA.ENABLE disables it at any time. CTRLA.SWRST resets every USB register and disables it.

operation.topic: USB device: attach, address and endpoints
operation.text: Clearing CTRLB.DETACH attaches the device to the bus and setting it detaches. The host reads the device descriptor at address 0, resets the bus and assigns an address, which software writes to DADD.DADD with DADD.ADDEN set; a bus reset clears ADDEN. Endpoint data can be anywhere in RAM: DESCADD holds the base address of the endpoint descriptor table, which the USB reads through its own AHB host. Before an endpoint is used its direction and type go into EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1, its descriptor is set to known values, PCKSIZE.SIZE to the size reported to the host, and ADDR to its data buffer. INTFLAG.RAMACER flags a RAM access underflow in an IN data stage. Disabling an endpoint clears its EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG and EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1.

Software gives the size and address of a RAM buffer and the USB splits it into as many packets as needed with no software action between them. OUT: PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT is zeroed and the total to receive written to PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE, which must be a multiple of PCKSIZE.SIZE or excess data may overwrite other SRAM; each full packet adds PCKSIZE.SIZE to BYTE_COUNT, and when BYTE_COUNT reaches MULTI_PACKET_SIZE the bank-ready and transfer-complete flags are set. IN: the total to send goes in BYTE_COUNT and MULTI_PACKET_SIZE starts at zero and counts bytes sent; each IN token sends PCKSIZE.SIZE bytes or the remainder, a short last packet ends the transfer, and with AUTOZLP set a zero-length packet follows when the total is a whole number of PCKSIZE.SIZE packets.

operation.topic: USB device: bus reset and start of frame
operation.text: A bus reset comes from the host and is handled in hardware. It clears EPCFG of every endpoint but endpoint 0, FNUM, DADD, EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG, EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1, EPINTSMRY and CTRLB.UPRSM, and sets INTFLAG.EORST when it ends. On each SOF token the frame number goes into FNUM.FNUM and INTFLAG.SOF is set; a CRC or bit-stuff error in it sets FNUM.FNCERR.

operation.topic: USB device: SETUP, OUT and IN transactions
operation.text: A token whose address does not match DADD.DADD, or that addresses a disabled endpoint or one of the wrong type, is ignored. SETUP: on a control endpoint the DATA0 packet is written to the ADDR buffer whenever EPINTFLAG.RXSTP is clear, regardless of BK0RDY; bytes past PCKSIZE.SIZE are dropped (the packet is still checked), so the size reported to the host must never exceed PCKSIZE.SIZE. On success the device ACKs, writes the byte count (CRC excluded) to PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT, sets DTGLOUT, DTGLIN, CURRBK and BK0RDY, clears BK1RDY and the stall requests, and sets RXSTP. OUT: a set STALLRQ0 returns STALL (non-isochronous) and sets STALL0; a data toggle mismatch discards the data but ACKs; a set BK0RDY discards the data, sets TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW and NAKs (non-isochronous); an isochronous packet with a CRC or bit-stuff error still has its byte count written and sets TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.CRCERR. A good OUT packet is ACKed (non-isochronous), counted, sets BK0RDY and TRCPT0 and toggles DTGLOUT. CRC bytes land in the buffer only when the packet is short: none for a full PCKSIZE.SIZE packet, one for a packet one byte short, both for two or more bytes short. IN: a set STALLRQ1 returns STALL and sets STALL1 (non-isochronous); a clear BK1RDY sets TRFAIL1 and NAKs (non-isochronous). Otherwise BYTE_COUNT bytes from ADDR are sent with CRC, as DATA0 on isochronous endpoints and DATA0 or DATA1 per DTGLIN on others. Isochronous IN then clears BK1RDY and sets TRCPT1 at once; others wait 16 bit times for the host's ACK, and on it clear BK1RDY, set TRCPT1 and toggle DTGLIN.

operation.topic: USB device: ping-pong and feedback endpoints
operation.text: Ping-pong operation uses both banks of an endpoint in one direction: one direction is enabled in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 and the other set to dual bank. The enabled endpoint's buffer, address and byte count are bank 0, the other direction's are bank 1, so software can work on one bank while the USB uses the other. EPSTATUS.CURBK names the bank for the next transaction and changes after each one; the flags of that bank are set, and the data toggles of the enabled direction alone are updated. A feedback endpoint shares an endpoint number with the first data endpoint it serves and runs the other direction, made by giving the IN and OUT halves different sizes and types: for example, endpoint n IN as interrupt IN with PCKSIZE.SIZE = 64 and endpoint n OUT as isochronous OUT with PCKSIZE.SIZE = 512.

operation.topic: USB device: suspend, wake-up and remote wake-up
operation.text: The pad has two states: idle (low power) and active. Detecting bus suspend sets INTFLAG.SUSPEND and puts the pad in idle; any non-idle bus state sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and wakes the pad. The pad also goes idle when the USB is disabled or CTRLB.DETACH is set, and returns to active when CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 and CTRLB.DETACH = 0. WAKEUP is an asynchronous interrupt that wakes the device from any sleep mode. Remote wake-up (upstream resume) is allowed only after SUSPEND has been set and the host has enabled it with DEVICE_REMOTE_WAKEUP; writing CTRLB.UPRSM sends it, and the controller sends it itself after 5 ms of bus inactivity. Sending it sets WAKEUP and clears SUSPEND; UPRSM clears when the resume has been sent, or at once if a host downstream resume is already under way. A host-rebroadcast resume sets INTFLAG.EORSM when it ends.

CTRLB.LPMHDSK sets the handshake given to an LPM transaction. When one arrives on an enabled endpoint (normally endpoint 0) the EXTREG field of that endpoint's bank 0 descriptor is filled with BESL, bRemoteWake and bLinkState. An ACK sets INTFLAG.LPMSUSP and the transceiver suspends 9 µs after the transaction; the USB clock can then be stopped, and the MCU can sleep in any mode whose wake-up time meets the host latency given by BESL. Leaving L1 is the same as leaving suspend, with a shorter remote wake-up. A NYET answer sets INTFLAG.LPMNYET; a STALL or no handshake sets nothing.

Each endpoint has flags STALL0/1, TRFAIL0/1, RXSTP and TRCPT0/1 in its EPINTFLAG, each gated by EPINTENSET; EPINTSMRY shows which endpoints have a pending interrupt. The device-wide INTFLAG holds LPMSUSP, LPMNYET, RAMACER, UPRSM, EORSM, WAKEUP, EORST, SOF, MSOF and SUSPEND, each gated by INTENSET. All of them combine into the one USB interrupt; WAKEUP is asynchronous.

operation.topic: USB host: connection, reset and pipes
operation.text: Software sets CTRLB.VBUSOK when VBUS is present; while it is clear, host operation is halted even when enabled. A device is detected by STATUS.LINESTATE when DP or DM is pulled high (which one tells the speed), and a disconnect when both are pulled low; these set INTFLAG.DCONN and INTFLAG.DDISC. In host mode an endpoint is called a pipe. CTRLB.BUSRESET sends a bus reset; when sent, INTFLAG.RST is set and all pipes are disabled; from suspend (CTRLB.SOFE = 0) it first resumes the bus, setting WAKEUP, and SOFE is set so SOFs start right after the reset. The reset clears every PCFG, FNUM, BINTERVAL, HSOFC, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and PSTATUS.FREEZE; STATUS.SPEED then gives the speed. Pipe descriptors, like endpoint descriptors, sit in RAM from DESCADD; each pipe is set up with its type in PCFG.PTYPE, PCKSIZE.SIZE as reported by the device, ADDR, and PCFG.BK for dual bank (not allowed on control pipes). Writing PTYPE non-zero enables a pipe and sets PSTATUS.FREEZE so it can be finished before transfers start; disabling one clears its BINTERVAL, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and FREEZE. The default control pipe size is reset from bMaxPacketSize0 in the device descriptor, and after SET_ADDRESS the new address goes into CTRL_PIPE.PDADDR in the pipe descriptor.

operation.topic: USB host: suspend, resume and phase-locked SOFs
operation.text: Clearing CTRLB.SOFE stops SOFs and the bus enters suspend; the device suspends 3 ms later. Active pipes are frozen first (PSTATUS.FREEZE), and at least one full frame should pass before suspend to avoid losing data. A non-idle bus sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP; an upstream resume (K state) also sets INTFLAG.UPRSM, and the host must answer with a downstream resume within 1 ms lasting at least 20 ms, started by setting CTRLB.RESUME. The host can also resume on its own with CTRLB.RESUME. When the downstream resume ends SOFE is set again. The SOF period is kept through active, idle, suspend and resume states (1 ms when active, a whole number of milliseconds otherwise) as long as GCLK_USB keeps running; if it stops the SOF period becomes erratic.

operation.topic: USB host: control, IN and OUT pipes
operation.text: A control transfer has SETUP, data and status stages; software sets PCFG.PTOKEN for each, and the initial data toggles are DATA0 for SETUP and DATA1 for IN and OUT. IN pipes: clearing PSTATUS.BK0/1RDY frees a bank, and IN requests run while the pipe is unfrozen. A full bank sets PINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1 and BK0/1RDY; software reads PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes from ADDR, clears TRCPT and BKRDY, and the next bank follows in dual-bank mode. PSTATUS.CURBK and DTGLIN show the current bank and toggle. Single bank uses only TRCPT0 and BK0. OUT pipes: software fills the ADDR buffer and sets BK0/1RDY to send it, clearing TRCPT0/1 first so no completion is missed. Several logical pipes can run one after another on one physical pipe by saving and restoring the pipe registers and descriptor (PCFG and PSTATUS above all).

Isochronous and interrupt pipes flag a data-flow error with PINTFLAG.TRFAIL: STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW in the bank descriptor marks an OUT underflow (sending from an empty bank) or an IN overflow (a packet arriving at a full bank, whose data is lost). Isochronous IN pipes flag a corrupted packet with TRFAIL and STATUS_BK.CRCERR; the packet stays in the bank and TRCPT is set. Any pipe sets PINTFLAG.PERR when an error field in STATUS_PIPE is set and STATUS_PIPE.ERCNT has passed CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX; below that the count just increments. PINTSMRY shows which pipe interrupted. A successful transaction clears ERRORFLOW.

Any enabled pipe with PCFG.PTYPE = EXTENDED sends an EXTENDED token followed by an LPM token (PTOKEN, BK and SIZE do not matter), using EXTREG.VARIABLE from the descriptor. An ACK puts the host in L1 sleep at once, for at least TL1RetryAndResidency, sets TRCPT0 and clears CTRLB.SOFE; NYET sets TRFAIL; STALL sets STALL. A missing or corrupted handshake repeats the token pair up to CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX times, then sets PERR and updates STATUS_BK. Every LPM outcome freezes the pipe. L1 is left by a downstream resume (CTRLB.RESUME) or an L1 resume (CTRLB.L1RESUME), whose K-state length comes from the BESL field of EXTREG.VARIABLE; a device upstream resume sets INTFLAG.UPRSM. SOFE is set again after resume.

Each pipe has flags STALL, PERR, TRFAIL, TXSTP and TRCPT0/1 in its PINTFLAG, each gated by PINTENSET; PINTSMRY shows which pipes are pending. The host INTFLAG holds DDISC, DCONN, RAMACER, UPRSM, DNRSM, WAKEUP, RST and HSOF, each gated by INTENSET. DDISC, DCONN and WAKEUP are asynchronous, and WAKEUP wakes the device from any sleep mode.

A 12-bit converter of up to 350 ksps, with 8-bit and 10-bit results for shorter conversions and accumulation, averaging and oversampling with decimation up to 16-bit results. Inputs are single-ended or differential: up to 32 analog inputs, 25 positive and 10 negative counting internal and external ones. The five internal inputs are the bandgap, the temperature sensor, the DAC, and the core and I/O supplies scaled down. A gain stage gives 1/2x to 16x. Conversions run single, continuous or as a pin scan, are started by software or by one event input, and results are signed or unsigned, left- or right-adjusted, and can be moved by DMA. A window monitor checks results against thresholds on a chosen channel, and gain and offset errors can be corrected in hardware. Conversion range: Vref from 1 V to VDDANA − 0.6 V; ADCx × GAIN from 0 V to −Vref. References: internal or external, chosen by four selection bits; INT1V is a buffered 1.0 V reference derived from the internal 1.1 V bandgap.

The input pins AIN0 to AIN19 and the VREFA/VREFB pins are set up in PORT. The ADC runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs, and every interrupt except OVERRUN can wake the device. The bus clock CLK_APB_ADC is enabled in the main clock; the generic clock GCLK_ADC must be set up in GCLK first and is asynchronous to the bus clock. One DMA request goes to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC and events to the event system. The ADC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless told to keep running. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG; PAC protection does not apply to debugger accesses. The production BIAS and LINEARITY calibration values must be copied from the NVM software calibration area into CALIB to reach the specified accuracy.

Before enabling, the GCLK_ADC source is chosen and enabled in SYSCTRL and the reference configured; the first conversion after a reference change must be discarded, and the other configuration must stay stable during a conversion. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the ADC on and off; CTRLA.SWRST, issued only while disabled, resets every register but DBGCTRL. The conversion rate follows GCLK_ADC and the prescaler, which divides it by 4 to 512 in powers of two (CTRLB.PRESCALER) to give CLK_ADC. A conversion starts on SWTRIG.START or on a trigger; with CTRLC.FREERUN = 1 conversions follow one another with no trigger. Each result overwrites RESULT; with more than one channel enabled it must be read as soon as INTFLAG.RESRDY sets or INTFLAG.OVERRUN flags data lost. RESRDY means the result has reached RESULT. Resolution is 8, 10 or 12 bits by CTRLB.RESSEL, 12 by default.

Differential mode (CTRLB.DIFFMODE) is the one to use when the positive input can fall below the negative input; single-ended conversion of an always-positive input gives the full 12-bit resolution. The negative input is tied to a ground: internal GND, IOGND or an external ground on a pin, chosen in CTRLB. Either kind runs single or free-running; in free-running mode INTFLAG.RESRDY sets after every conversion. A conversion begins once the software or event start has been synchronized to GCLK_ADC, and sampling takes the first half of a CLK_ADC cycle. SAMPCTRL.SAMPLEN lengthens the sampling time. Single-ended conversions include an amplify phase after sampling.

AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM sets how many consecutive results are added together (1 to 1024). Beyond 16 samples the sum would overflow the 16-bit RESULT, so it is shifted right automatically. Accumulating two or more samples needs CTRLB.RESSEL set. Averaging divides the sum by the sample count: the automatic shift plus an extra shift written to AVGCTRL.ADJRES. It improves accuracy in noise at the cost of rate: the averaged rate is the un-averaged rate divided by the sample count, and RESRDY sets when the average is ready. Averaging two or more samples needs CTRLB.RESSEL = 1.

Oversampling raises the resolution from 12 bits up to 16 bits at a lower effective rate: n extra bits need 4^n samples accumulated and the sum shifted right n places, the shift being the automatic one plus AVGCTRL.ADJRES.

WINCTRL.WINMODE[2:0] picks the window condition and WINLT and WINUT hold the lower and upper thresholds. They are compared as signed values in differential mode and unsigned otherwise, using only as many bits as CTRLB.RESSEL gives (the low eight in 8-bit mode); in differential 8-bit mode the eighth bit is the sign even when the ninth is zero. A match sets INTFLAG.WINMON.

Offset error is how far the transfer function sits from the ideal line at zero input; gain error is how far the midpoint of the last output step sits from the ideal line once offset is removed. With CTRLB.CORREN set, OFFSETCORR is subtracted from each conversion and the difference scaled by GAINCORR before it is written to RESULT. The correction adds 13 CLK_ADC cycles of latency: on every conversion in single-conversion mode, on the first one only in free-running mode.

One DMA request, RESRDY, sets when a result (or a finished average) is ready and clears when RESULT is read. Interrupt sources are RESRDY, WINMON and OVERRUN, each with a flag in INTFLAG and enabled through INTENSET/INTENCLR. Output events are RESRDY and WINMON (EVCTRL.xxEO); input events START a conversion or FLUSH it (EVCTRL.xxEI). With several events routed to the ADC, the enabled action follows any of them.

With CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 0 the ADC is off in standby, keeping its configuration, and its analog blocks are powered down, so it needs a start-up delay on wake-up. With RUNSTDBY = 1 it keeps converting and any enabled interrupt but OVERRUN wakes the CPU; while the CPU sleeps only events can start conversions. CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE, and the registers CTRLB, SWTRIG, WINCTRL, INPUTCTRL, WINUT and WINLT, are synchronized when written; SWTRIG and INPUTCTRL are synchronized when read. STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set during synchronization; an access needing synchronization while it is set stalls the bus until done, holding off the CPU and interrupts.

Up to four comparators in pairs: COMP0 and COMP1, and on 'L' variant devices a second pair COMP2 and COMP3 (the AC1 module). Each compares two inputs and gives a digital output, '1' when the positive input is above the negative. Hysteresis is adjustable, and each pair can work as a window comparator. Inputs: four pins shared by a pair, each usable on either side, ground (to detect zero crossings), the bandgap reference, a 64-level VDD scaler per comparator and the DAC. Outputs can go to pins, synchronous or not. Interrupts on rising edge, falling edge, toggle or end of comparison; window interrupts on above, inside, below or outside; events from the comparator output and the window state; and an optional digital filter.

The AC runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs, and its interrupts wake the device. The bus clock CLK_AC_APB is gated in the main clock module. Two generic clocks serve it: GCLK_AC_DIG sets the comparator sampling rate, and GCLK_AC_ANA is needed when VDDANA is below 2.5 V to keep the input multiplexer resistance low; both are set up in GCLK first and are asynchronous to the bus clock. There is no DMA; interrupts go to the NVIC and events to the event system. The AC keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless told to halt. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except CTRLB and INTFLAG; PAC protection does not apply to debugger accesses. Each pair shares four I/O pins as analog inputs, which are set for analog use first; an internal source such as the bandgap or the DAC is enabled before it is used as an input.

EVCTRL (input and output events) is set before enabling and cannot change while the AC is enabled. CTRLA.ENABLE and CTRLA.SWRST enable and reset the whole AC. Each comparator is configured in COMPCTRLx before its own COMPCTRLx.ENABLE is set, and cannot be changed while enabled: SINGLE (measurement mode), HYST (hysteresis), SPEED (speed against power), INTSEL (interrupt source), MUXPOS and MUXNEG (inputs), FLEN (filter) and RUNSTDBY. Disabling the AC disables every comparator without clearing their ENABLE bits.

After enabling, a start-up time, measured automatically to follow temperature and supply, passes before the first result; the output is not available during it. Continuous mode (SINGLE = 0) compares all the time: STATUSA.STATEx always holds the latest result, STATUSB.READYx sets after the start-up time, and edges are found by comparing successive samples at the CLK_AC_DIG rate. In sleep it can run with no clock: changes are seen asynchronously and the Power Manager starts CLK_AC_DIG only to register events and interrupts. Single-shot mode (SINGLE = 1) leaves the comparator idle until CTRLB.STARTx is written (which clears READYx), until STATUSC is read (which starts every single-shot comparator and stalls the bus until all are ready, or waits for one already busy), or until an input event enabled by EVCTRL.COMPEIx arrives. After the start-up time one comparison is made, STATUSA updated and READYx set. The interrupt can be set by INTSEL for toggle, rising edge, falling edge or end of comparison; events follow the output state whether or not interrupts are enabled. Enabling takes 2 to 3 GCLK_AC cycles before the start-up time begins.

The positive input is one of the AINx pins, chosen by COMPCTRLx.MUXPOS; the negative input is an AINx pin or one of the internal sources shared by all comparators, chosen by COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG. An external pin is set for analog use in PORT, its digital input and output disabled. The multiplexers switch so as to keep crosstalk low, and the selection is changed only while the comparator is disabled. For the CCL to use a comparison result internally, the field is 0x1 or 0x2.

WINCTRL.WENx joins a pair into a window comparator. Both comparators take the same pin as positive input and must have the same SINGLE setting; their negative inputs set the upper and lower limits, in either order. STATUS.WSTATEx gives the window state, and WINCTRL.WINTSEL picks an interrupt on going above, below, into or out of the window. Events follow inside/outside whether or not the interrupt is enabled, and each comparator's own outputs, interrupts and events still work. In single-shot window mode both comparators measure together, started by either STARTx bit or either event.

operation.topic: AC voltage doubler and VDDANA scaler
operation.text: A voltage doubler lowers the analog multiplexer resistance when the supply is below 2.5 V; it switches on and off by supply level and adds settling time when the comparators are enabled. When the supply stays above 2.5 V, CTRLA.LPMUX = 1 turns it off, saving power and shortening start-up. The VDDANA scaler gives each comparator its own reference, a fraction of the supply in 64 steps set by SCALERx.VALUE; it is on when COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG = 0x5 and the comparator is enabled.

Hysteresis (COMPCTRLx.HYSTEN) is set per comparator and works only in continuous mode. COMPCTRLx.SPEED sets the bias current and so trades propagation delay against power, and also changes the start-up time. A digital filter set by COMPCTRLx.FLEN is off, a 3-sample majority or a 5-sample majority: a change counts when N/2 + 1 of the last N samples agree, sampled at the GCLK_AC rate. It adds N − 1 sample periods of delay: in continuous mode the first valid output comes after N samples and then one every cycle; in single-shot mode the comparison ends at the Nth sample. In sleep, filtering works only for single-shot measurements and must be off for continuous measurements during sleep, or interrupts and events may be wrong.

COMPCTRLx.OUT routes a comparator to its CMP[x] pin, either raw and unsynchronized or synchronized to CLK_AC with filtering. COMPCTRLx.SWAP exchanges the positive and negative inputs and inverts the output, so the input offset voltage can be measured or cancelled; the output inverts only when the input difference is within the offset. SWAP is changed only while the comparator is disabled.

Interrupt sources: COMP0 to COMP3 (status change as chosen by INTSEL) and WIN0, WIN1 (window change as chosen by WINCTRL.WINTSELx), each with an INTFLAG flag and enabled by INTENSET/INTENCLR, all combined into one NVIC request. Output events COMP0 to COMP3 copy the comparator state and WIN0, WIN1 the window state, each enabled by EVCTRL.COMPEOx. An input event enabled by EVCTRL.COMPEIx starts a single-shot measurement after the start-up time; in window mode either event starts both comparators.

Each COMPCTRLx.RUNSTDBY sets one comparator's standby behaviour. At 0 the comparator is off in standby, keeping its configuration, with its analog blocks powered down, so it needs a start-up delay on wake-up. At 1 it keeps working and any enabled AC interrupt wakes the CPU; single-shot comparisons can then be started only by events. The AC works in sleep with its clock off as long as it stays powered. Continuous mode then runs asynchronously: a matching edge starts GCLK_AC_DIG to register the interrupt and events, waking the device if the interrupt is enabled, with no filtering. Single-shot mode starts GCLK_AC_DIG on an event, waits the start-up time, compares (with filtering allowed) and turns the comparator and clock off again unless set to wake the system.
CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE and COMPCTRLn.ENABLE, and the WINCTRL register, are synchronized when written.

One 10-bit channel converting up to 350 ksps, with several trigger sources, a high-drive output buffer, DMA support, and an output that can feed the analog comparator and the ADC. The reference is the internal reference (the default), VDDANA or the external VREFA pin, chosen by CTRLB.REFSEL; the output spans GND to the reference.

The DAC runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs, and its interrupts wake the device. The bus clock CLK_DAC_APB is gated by the Power Manager; the generic clock GCLK_DAC must be set up in GCLK first and is asynchronous to the bus clock. A DMA request goes to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC and events to the event system. When the CPU is halted by a debugger the DAC halts after finishing any conversion, unless told to keep running. Every writable register can be PAC write-protected except INTFLAG and DATABUF; PAC protection does not apply to debugger accesses. VOUT and VREFA are configured first, and an internal input is enabled before the DAC.

CTRLB and EVCTRL can be written only while the DAC is disabled, and CTRLB.REFSEL is set before enabling. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the DAC on and off; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and disables it. CTRLB.EOEN enables the output driver on VOUT, which drives resistive and capacitive loads; it is best left off when no external output is needed, to save power. Writing DATA, by the CPU or DMA, starts a conversion, as does a START event that loads DATA from DATABUF. Nothing signals the end of a conversion, so the sample period must be at least the specified conversion time.

DMA request EMPTY sets when DATABUF moves into the DAC's internal buffer and clears when DATABUF is written or INTFLAG.EMPTY is cleared; since DATABUF starts empty, a request is made as soon as the DAC is enabled. CPU access to the registers behind a DMA request can lose it or corrupt the transfer. With the DAC PAC-protected, DATABUF can still be written when CTRLB.BDWP = 1. Interrupts: EMPTY (internal buffer empty), UNDERRUN (a start event while the buffer was empty) and SYNCRDY (asynchronous, wakes the device from any sleep mode), each flagged in INTFLAG and enabled by INTENSET/INTENCLR, combined into one NVIC request. Output event EMPTY is enabled by EVCTRL.EMPTYEO. Input event START (EVCTRL.STARTEI) moves DATABUF into DATA when the DAC is ready and converts it; it is resynchronized to GCLK_DAC. With start events in use only DATABUF is written, never DATA. Input events act on a rising edge by default; EVCTRL.INVEIx = 1 makes them act on a falling one, and any of several connected events triggers the action.

GCLK_DAC runs in idle sleep. In standby the output buffer holds its value when CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1 and is disabled when it is 0. CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE and every bit of DATA and DATABUF are synchronized when written; nothing is synchronized when read. STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set during synchronization, and an access needing synchronization while it is set is discarded with an error.

operation.topic: DAC internal output, data buffer and voltage pump
operation.text: CTRLB.IOEN feeds the DAC output to the analog comparator, at the same time as the external output if wanted; to feed the ADC the output buffer must be on. DATABUF and DATA form a two-stage FIFO: a start event moves DATABUF into DATA and starts a conversion, an empty DATABUF at that moment raises UNDERRUN, and the EMPTY event and interrupt say DATABUF can take new data. Below 2.5 V the voltage pump must run; it is turned on automatically by supply level and can be turned off with CTRLB.VPD = 1 above 2.5 V to save power. The pump runs from GCLK_DAC, whose frequency must be at least four times the sampling rate.

The Peripheral Touch Controller measures capacitive sensors whose electrodes, usually on the PCB, connect straight to I/O pins, one pin per electrode with no external parts. Mutual-capacitance sensing uses an X-Y matrix (ITO grids included), one pin per X line and one per Y line; self-capacitance needs one Y pin per sensor; both kinds can be mixed. Buttons: 6, 10 or 16 in self-capacitance and 60, 120 or 256 in mutual capacitance on 32-, 48- and 64-pin devices. It compensates parasitic capacitance, has adjustable gain, auto-calibrates against temperature and VDD drift, filters noise and desynchronizes it in hardware, has a selectable channel-change settling delay, starts acquisition on command or automatically, interrupts on completion, and can wake the device on touch from standby. The acquisition module holds gain control, an ADC and filtering, gives a 10-bit result, and has a series resistance RS of 0, 20, 50 or 100 kΩ. It is used through the QTouch Library, configured with the QTouch Configurator and linked into the application, for buttons, sliders and wheels.

Each X and Y line connects to a sensor electrode; no external parts are needed, but a series resistor of 1 kΩ or more on the X and Y lines improves EMC. A mutual-capacitance sensor is the capacitance between an X (transmit) electrode and a Y (sense) electrode; a self-capacitance sensor is one Y electrode's capacitance. GCLK_PTC clocks the PTC, asynchronous to the system and bus clocks, from a source chosen in GCLK and enabled in the Power Manager (off by default); its range is 400 kHz to 4 MHz.

operation.topic: Electrical characteristics: typical and limit values
operation.text: Typical values are at 25 °C unless a row says otherwise; minimum and maximum values hold over the whole operating temperature and voltage range unless a row says otherwise. The part comes in four temperature grades: 85 °C (TA −40 °C to 85 °C, TJ up to 100 °C), 105 °C (TJ up to 125 °C), 125 °C (TJ up to 145 °C) and AEC-Q100 125 °C. Some figures differ by device variant (A; B, C, D, L) or by silicon revision (E, F, G).

Stress above the absolute maximum ratings can destroy the part; operation at those levels is not implied, and long exposure to them can reduce reliability. The part is ESD sensitive. In debugger cold-plugging mode NVM erase is not protected by BOD33 or BOD12, and erasing with the supply below its minimum can corrupt NVM areas the device needs to run correctly.

VDDIO, VDDIN and VDDANA all accept 1.62 V to 3.63 V across −40 °C to 85 °C (junction up to 100 °C), and each may rise at no more than 0.1 V/μs. The 1.62 V minimum holds with BOD33 off; with BOD33 on, the BOD33 level sets the minimum.

Active, idle and standby currents are measured at VDDIN = 3.3 V (or 1.8 V where stated, with the CPU on flash at three wait states). XOSC is off; XOSC32K runs with an external 32 kHz crystal; DFLL48M runs at 48 MHz locked to XOSC32K and is the main clock unless stated. CPU and AHB clocks are undivided, APBA is divided by 4 and the APBB and APBC bridges are off. Only the NVMCTRL and APBA bridge AHB clocks and the PM, SYSCTRL and RTC peripheral clocks run. I/Os are inactive with pull-ups on, the CPU runs from flash at one wait state, the cache is on and BOD33 is off. Wake-up time runs from the wake-up signal edge to the first instruction fetched from flash.

Peripheral currents are measured at VDDIN = 3.3 V with XOSC off, XOSC32K running from a 32 kHz crystal and OSC8M at 8 MHz as the undivided main clock. Only the NVMCTRL and HPB0-HPB2 bridge AHB clocks and the PM and SYSCTRL clocks run; I/Os are inactive with pull-ups, the CPU sits in IDLE0, the cache is on and BOD33 is off. The baseline current is taken in this state; then for each peripheral its GCLK is set up, its clock unmasked, it is enabled, the CPU enters IDLE0 and the current is measured, the CPU is woken through the EIC (asynchronous level detection, no filter), and the peripheral is disabled and its clocks removed. Each table entry is the measured current minus the baseline.

USB currents are measured at VDDIN = 3.3 V. In device mode the DFLL48M runs in USB recovery mode without a crystal; in host mode the DFLL48M runs in closed loop from XOSC32K with a 32 kHz crystal. CPU, AHB and APBn clocks are undivided, only the NVMCTRL and HPB0-HPB2 bridge AHB clocks run, I/Os are inactive with pull-ups, the CPU is in IDLE0, the cache is on and BOD33 is off. The USB states follow the USB 2.0 standard.

operation.topic: I2C, XOSC, XOSC32 and reset pins
operation.text: The I2C pins are listed in the I/O multiplexing table and their timing is in the SERCOM I2C timing tables. Used as plain I/O, the XOSC and XOSC32 pins behave as normal I/O pins, and the RESET pin has the electrical characteristics of a normal I/O pin.

Injected pin current is a stress rating like the absolute maximum ratings. Up to ±1 mA per pin (Iinj1) is allowed when 3 V < VDD ≤ 3.6 V, up to ±15 mA per pin (Iinj2) when VDD ≤ 3 V, and the sum over all pins is limited to ±45 mA. When a pin is driven below GND − 0.6 V or above VDD + 0.6 V a series resistor must limit the current; injection can affect the accuracy of the analog blocks.

The ADC can average several consecutive conversions to raise accuracy; AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM[3:0] sets the number of samples and the averaged value appears in RESULT. Offset and gain errors can be cancelled in hardware: OFFSETCORR holds the offset correction and GAINCORR the gain correction, applied to the conversion before it is written to RESULT.

Seen from outside, an ADC input is a series resistance RSAMPLE and a sampling capacitance CSAMPLE (referred to VDDANA/2). The source must charge CSAMPLE to within the required accuracy during the sampling time, so the source resistance RSOURCE adds to RSAMPLE when the sampling time is chosen.

The temperature sensor output is linear but depends on the internal reference, which itself drifts with temperature. Each device stores a temperature log row at 0x00806030, written during production test at a room and a hot insertion. It was measured with VDDIN = VDDIO = VDDANA = 3.3 V, ADC clock 1 MHz, free-running mode averaging 4 samples, reference INT1V and the temperature sensor as input. It holds each insertion's temperature (integer and decimal parts, e.g. 25 and 2 for 25.2 °C), the 12-bit ADC result at that temperature, and the INT1V value then as a two's complement offset from 1 V in 1 mV steps. Software uses these points to interpolate first a coarse temperature, then INT1V at that temperature, then a finer temperature.
In the 85 °C and 125 °C ranges a flash row accepts at most 8 consecutive writes before it must be erased; in the 105 °C range the limit is 4 consecutive writes.

With a crystal between XIN and XOUT, choose a crystal whose load capacitance CL is within the table range; the exact CL is in the crystal's data sheet. The external capacitors CLEXT then follow from the load capacitance equation, counting the XIN and XOUT pin capacitances and the board stray capacitance. The XOSC32K crystal uses the same connection and equation.

PTC currents are measured at VDD = 3.3 V with OSC8M undivided at 8 MHz as the main clock, the CPU on flash with zero wait states at 8 MHz and the PTC at 4 MHz, in mutual-capacitance mode with one touch channel and standby sleep enabled. The RTC, clocked from OSCULP32K, sets the scan rate through the event system. With drift calibration disabled there are no interrupts and scans run in standby; with drift calibration enabled the RTC wakes the CPU to run the scans and drift calibration runs every 1.5 s.

The USB buffers meet the USB 2.0 standard, whose electrical specification gives the AC parameters. The interface is USB-IF certified as a low/full-speed peripheral silicon building block (TID 40001583) and as a full-speed embedded host (TID 120000272). For compliance the CPU clock must be above 8 MHz while USB is active (no limit in suspend), the supply must be 3.3 V (3.0 V to 3.6 V), and GCLK_USB must be 48 MHz within ±0.25 % in device mode or ±0.05 % in host mode. The 105 °C and 125 °C ranges share these USB characteristics.

As for the 85 °C range except for the clocks: XOSC32K is off, XOSC runs from an external 32 MHz clock on XIN and is the main clock, and DFLL48M is off. VDDIN = 3.3 V. Standby figures are taken with the regulator kept on (VREG.RUNSTDBY = 1).

operation.topic: Current consumption test conditions (125 °C and AEC-Q100)
operation.text: As for the 85 °C range: VDDIN = 3.3 V, XOSC off, XOSC32K running from a 32 kHz crystal, DFLL48M at 48 MHz locked to XOSC32K as the main clock, CPU and AHB undivided, APBA divided by 4, APBB and APBC off, flash at one wait state, cache on, BOD33 off. Standby figures are taken with VREG.RUNSTDBY = 1.

In the AEC-Q100 set VDD and VDDANA run from 2.7 V to 3.63 V over −40 °C to 125 °C with the junction up to 145 °C. Supplies may rise at up to 0.1 V/μs and fall at up to 0.05 V/μs, and BOD33 should be enabled to secure power-up and power-down. Junction temperature follows the same two equations as the other grades.
Every part is tested in production to run the CPU from the DFLL48M in closed loop, referenced either to an external oscillator or to the internal OSC8M.

operation.topic: Debugger cold-plug and NVM erase (SAM DA1)
operation.text: When a debugger cold-plugs the part, NVM erase operations are not guarded by BOD33 or BOD12. Erasing with the supply below its specified minimum can corrupt NVM areas the device needs to run correctly. The part is ESD sensitive.

Figures are measured with VDDIN at 3.3 V (and at 2.7 V with the CPU running from flash at one wait state). XOSC is off, XOSC32K runs from an external 32 kHz crystal and the DFLL48M, referenced to XOSC32K, runs at 48 MHz as the main clock. CPU and AHB clocks are undivided, APBA is divided by 4 and the APBB and APBC bridges are off. Only the NVMCTRL and APBA bridge AHB clocks and the PM, SYSCTRL and RTC peripheral clocks run. I/Os are inactive with pull-ups on, the CPU runs from flash at one wait state with the cache on, and BOD33 is off. Wake-up time runs from the wake-up signal edge to the first instruction fetched from flash.

Each peripheral figure is Iperiph − Idefault. The baseline Idefault is taken with VDDIN at 3.3 V, XOSC off, XOSC32K running on a 32 kHz crystal and OSC8M at 8 MHz as the main clock, CPU, AHB and APB clocks undivided, only the NVMCTRL and HPB0 to HPB2 bridge AHB clocks and the PM and SYSCTRL clocks on, I/Os inactive with pull-ups, the CPU in IDLE0 with the cache on and BOD33 off. For each peripheral its GCLK is set up and enabled where it has one, its clock unmasked and the peripheral enabled; the CPU then enters IDLE0, Iperiph is measured, and the CPU is woken through the EIC (asynchronous level detection, no filter) before everything is undone.

operation.topic: XOSC, XOSC32K and RESET pins as I/O (SAM DA1)
operation.text: Used as general I/O, the XOSC and XOSC32K pins have the normal I/O pin characteristics, and RESET behaves electrically like a normal I/O pin too.

operation.topic: Power-on reset and BOD33 thresholds (SAM DA1)
operation.text: The internal reset is released when VDD rises through VPOT+ and asserted again when it falls below VPOT-. With BOD33 hysteresis off, reset follows VDD crossing the single level VBOD in either direction; with hysteresis on, VDD must rise above VBOD+ to release reset and fall below VBOD- to assert it.

operation.topic: ADC averaging and offset/gain correction (SAM DA1)
operation.text: The ADC can average a run of consecutive conversions in hardware to raise accuracy; AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM[3:0] sets how many, and the average lands in RESULT. Offset and gain errors can be removed in hardware: the values in OFFSETCORR and GAINCORR are applied to each conversion before it is written to RESULT.

From outside, an ADC input looks like the series resistance RSAMPLE into the sampling capacitor CSAMPLE, which is referred to VDDANA/2. The source resistance RSOURCE adds to RSAMPLE, and the source must charge CSAMPLE within the sampling time for full accuracy.
On this flash at most 8 consecutive writes may be made to a row; after the eighth the row must be erased before it is written again.

The USB buffers meet USB 2.0, whose electrical specification holds their AC parameters, and the interface is USB-IF certified (TID 40001583, low/full-speed peripheral silicon building block; TID 120000272, full-speed embedded host). For compliance the CPU must run above 8 MHz while USB is active (no limit in suspend), the supply must be 3.3 V (3.0 V to 3.6 V), and GCLK_USB must be 48 MHz within ±0.25 % in device mode or ±0.05 % in host mode.

In host mode, MISO setup and hold (tMIS, tMIH) are taken at the sampling SCK edge and MOSI setup and hold (tMOS, tMOH) at the launching edge; SCK has period tSCK, high and low widths tSCKW and rise and fall tSCKR, tSCKF, for CPOL 0 or 1. In client mode SS must lead the first SCK edge by tSSS and trail the last by tSSH; MOSI setup and hold are tSIS, tSIH; MISO is valid tSOSS after SS falls, set up tSOS before SCK, and held tSOSH after SS rises.

SWDCLK high and low periods are Thigh and Tlow. In a read the part drives SWDIO with skew Tos from the falling SWDCLK edge; in a write SWDIO from the debugger needs setup Tis and hold Tih around the rising edge.

The -SLL ordering codes are IEC 61508 SIL 2 enabled parts that can run Microchip's SIL 2 certified self-test library (STL), supplied on request with its user's manual and an integration checklist; the Embex SIL 2 Library User's Manual covers its use. Other SIL 2 enabled codes can be requested.

The -AZ510 and -AZT510 ordering codes carry a full ISELED license and can use Microchip's ISELED software stack and library (source, header, binary and user's manual). The ISELED control commands are those of the Inova INLC10AQ (document AN-INLC_04). Other ISELED codes can be requested.
Every device carries the Atmel logo and its ordering code, plus a line giving the manufacturing year (YY), manufacturing week (WW), an internal code (R) and the lot number (XXXXXX).

In an electromagnetically noisy setting the part needs protecting from that noise beyond normal EMC practice. Decoupling capacitors placed right at the power pins, an RC filter on RESET and a pull-up on SWCLK are singled out as critical, and noise should be kept from reaching the supply pins, I/O pins and crystals.

The SAM D21 runs from one supply of 1.62 V to 3.63 V. VDDIO, VDDIN and VDDANA each get 100 nF plus 10 μF; a 10 μH inductor can filter the incoming supply into VDD, and a ferrite bead between VDD and VDDANA keeps digital noise out of the analog domain. A suitable bead has a low DC resistance and enough impedance, such as 50 Ω at 20 MHz and 220 Ω at 100 MHz. VDDCORE (1.6 V to 1.8 V) takes 1 μF. All values are typical examples; each decoupling capacitor goes close to its supply pin pair, and low-ESR ceramic or solid tantalum parts are preferred.

External references are needed only when an external reference is used. An AREFx pin takes 1.0 V to VDDANA − 0.6 V for the ADC or the DAC, decoupled with 100 nF close to the pin and 4.7 μF (typical values). With one reference, AREFA and AREFB can be tied together on it, each pin keeping its own 100 nF.

The reset network is needed only when something drives RESET low; the switch can be left off if no manual reset is wanted, and an external pull-up is optional because RESET has an internal one. A pull-up keeps RESET from dropping by accident. The resistor in series with the switch lets the filter capacitor discharge gently, avoiding a current surge and the noise spike it would cause. The variant with 100 pF across a 2.2 kΩ pull-up is aimed at fast transient (EFT) immunity; slow glitches pass it, so it is no button debouncer.

The part can run from internal clocks, external clocks or a mix, for example OSC8M as the system clock with a 32.768 kHz watch crystal clocking the RTC. An external clock goes into XIN, leaving XOUT free to be left open or used as a GPIO. A crystal belongs as close to the part as possible: long lines add load the oscillator may not drive and couple noise into other circuits.

XOSC32K is built for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal and for very low power, so the crystal's load capacitance and ESR, both from the crystal maker, need care. The oscillator's internal load capacitance plus board capacitance lets a crystal of under 12.5 pF load run with no external capacitors; adding CLEXT on XIN32 and XOUT32 improves accuracy and safety factor. To keep the cycle-to-cycle jitter low, the pins next to the oscillator pins should be kept as quiet as possible.
Unused pins need no configuration: their reset state already gives the lowest leakage current.

Programming and debugging use the Serial Wire Debug interface, supported by Microchip tools such as JTAGICE3, SAM-ICE and Atmel-ICE, by the embedded debugger on the SAM D21 Xplained Pro kit (which needs no external tool), and by third-party debuggers. A pull-up on SWCLK (1 kΩ) is critical for reliable operation. A Cortex Debug 10-pin header connects SWDIO, SWDCLK, nRESET, VTref and ground; the JTAGICE3 needs its own 10-pin layout or its squid cable; a 20-pin IDC JTAG header (for example for SAM-ICE) uses pins 7, 9 and 15 for SWDIO, SWDCLK and nRESET, and its GND* pins may be left open or grounded.

USB uses the D+/D- differential pair plus VBUS and GND; the operating voltage range that allows USB is in the electrical characteristics. The pair should be impedance matched, routed with equal length, width and via count, kept parallel with as few bends and vias as possible. Dedicated transient suppressors on D+, D- and VBUS, placed close to the connector, improve ESD robustness. Tying the cable shield straight to ground makes the cable an antenna; an RC filter (1 MΩ with 4.5 nF) between shield and ground limits that.
